title: Plant parts: how each part's shape suits its job

summary.text: A potato grows under the ground, but it is a stem, not a root. Its eyes are buds, and buds grow on stems. Every part of a plant has a shape that suits its job. Thin roots reach between soil grains to soak up water, and fat roots and stems store food. Climbing stems are thin and hold on to a support, and flat leaves spread out to catch sunlight. In deserts, ponds and salty mud, the parts take new shapes to fit.
summary.art: One plant with their parts labelled: fat carrot-like roots storing food underground, a stem twining up a stick, a tendril curling round a string, and wide flat leaves tilted towards the Sun.

intro.hook: Look at a carrot and a potato. Both grow under the ground. Both are fat and full of food. But only one of them is a root. Which one? And how could you ever tell?
intro.text: A carrot and a potato look alike, but they are different parts of a plant. The carrot is a root. The potato is a stem that grows under the ground. Its 'eyes' show this, because only stems have buds like that. In this unit you will learn to tell each part by its clues, not by where it grows. You will also find out why each part of a plant has the shape it has.
intro.art: A carrot and a potato side by side on a kitchen board, a magnifying glass over the potato's eyes, a question mark between them.

outcomes: I can name the parts of a plant and say the main job of each one.
I can explain how a part's shape suits its job, with examples from roots, stems and leaves.
I can tell a root from a stem, even under the ground, using clues like eyes, rings and buds.
I can give examples of roots and stems that store food, stems that climb and leaves that catch light, and say how each one helps the plant.
I can run a fair test, measure carefully, and show my results in a table and a bar chart.
I can explain how plants in hard places, like deserts, ponds and salty mud, have parts with special shapes.
I can say what scientists agree on about plant shapes and what they still argue about. I can link plant shapes to light, atoms, the history of the Earth and even other planets.

terms.meaning: The part of a plant that is usually under the ground. It holds the plant in the soil and soaks up water.
terms.example: Pull up a weed from a crack in the wall. The thin white threads at the bottom are their roots.
terms.art: A small weed pulled up from a crack, their thin white roots holding a crumb of soil.

terms.meaning: The part that holds the plant up and joins the roots to the leaves. Water travels up it from the roots, and food from the leaves travels through it to the rest of the plant.
terms.example: A tree trunk is a stem. So is the soft green stalk of a coriander plant.
terms.art: A tree trunk next to a thin green coriander stalk, both labelled stem.

terms.meaning: The usually flat, green part of a plant. Leaves catch sunlight and use it to make the plant's food.
terms.example: A mango leaf, a tulsi leaf and a blade of grass are all leaves.
terms.art: Three leaves in a row: mango, tulsi and a blade of grass.

terms.meaning: What a part does for the plant. Scientists call it the part's function.
terms.example: The job of a root is to hold the plant in the soil and soak up water. The job of a leaf is to catch light.
terms.art: A root with a little anchor icon and a leaf with a little sun icon.

terms.meaning: Each part of a plant has a shape that helps it do its job well. Scientists say form fits function.
terms.example: Leaves are thin and flat to catch lots of light. Roots are long and thin to reach far into the soil.
terms.art: A thin flat leaf facing the Sun and a long thin root reaching down between soil grains.

terms.meaning: A shape or habit that helps a living thing survive where they live.
terms.example: A cactus has spines instead of wide leaves. That helps them keep water in the hot desert.
terms.art: A spiny cactus in a hot sandy desert under a blazing Sun.

terms.meaning: One thick main root that grows straight down, with thinner roots growing out of its sides.
terms.example: Mustard, neem and carrot plants have tap roots.
terms.art: A mustard seedling pulled up, showing one long main root with small side roots.

terms.meaning: A bunch of many thin roots, all about the same size, spreading out like a beard.
terms.example: Grass, wheat, rice and onions have fibrous roots.
terms.art: A tuft of grass pulled up, showing a beard of thin roots holding soil.

terms.meaning: A tiny hair on a young root. Root hairs push between soil grains and soak up water.
terms.example: Look at a moong sprout's root against black paper. The white fuzz is root hairs.
terms.art: A moong sprout's root against black paper, covered in fine white fuzz.

terms.meaning: A root that grows fat because it is full of stored food.
terms.example: Carrot, radish, beetroot and shakarkand, which is sweet potato, are storage roots.
terms.art: A carrot, a radish, a beetroot and a sweet potato lying in a row.

terms.meaning: A tiny folded-up shoot, waiting to grow into new leaves, a branch or a flower. Buds grow on stems, not usually on roots.
terms.example: The 'eyes' of a potato are buds. Leave an old potato in a dark basket and they grow shoots.
terms.art: An old potato with pale shoots growing from its eyes.

terms.meaning: The place on a stem where a leaf or a bud grows. Nodes often look like rings or bumps.
terms.example: The rings on sugarcane and on a piece of ginger are nodes.
terms.art: A piece of sugarcane and a piece of ginger with their rings circled.

terms.meaning: A fat underground stem that stores food. It has buds, called eyes, that can grow into new plants.
terms.example: A potato is a tuber.
terms.art: A potato plant dug up, with potatoes hanging from underground stems.

terms.meaning: A stem that grows sideways under the ground. It stores food and has rings and buds.
terms.example: Ginger and turmeric (manjal, or haldi) are rhizomes.
terms.art: A knobbly piece of ginger with its rings and a small green shoot.

terms.meaning: A tiny flat stem with thick, juicy leaves wrapped round it. The leaves store food.
terms.example: An onion is a bulb. Each layer you peel is the swollen bottom of a leaf.
terms.art: An onion cut in half from top to bottom, showing its layers and the flat stem at the bottom.

terms.meaning: A plant with a thin stem that grows upwards by holding on to something else.
terms.example: Money plant, bean, grape and bottle gourd are climbers.
terms.art: A money plant climbing up a pole, holding on with little roots.

terms.meaning: A climber whose stem winds round and round a support, like a spiral staircase.
terms.example: A bean plant twines round a stick.
terms.art: A bean stem spiralling round a bamboo stick.

terms.meaning: A thin, curly thread that a climbing plant uses to grab hold of things. It coils when it touches something.
terms.example: Pea and bottle gourd plants have tendrils.
terms.art: A gourd tendril coiled tightly round a string, like a spring.

terms.meaning: A root that grows in the air, out of a stem or branch, instead of under the ground.
terms.example: A banyan tree's hanging roots, and the roots a money plant uses to climb, are aerial roots.
terms.art: A banyan tree with long roots hanging down from their branches like ropes.

terms.meaning: A root that grows down from the stem or a branch into the ground, and holds the plant up like a pillar.
terms.example: Old banyan trees stand on many pillar roots. Maize and sugarcane have short prop roots near the ground.
terms.art: The base of a maize plant with short roots coming out of the stem and pushing into the soil like tent pegs.

terms.meaning: A root that sticks up out of wet mud into the air, so the plant can get air to their roots.
terms.example: Mangrove trees in the Sundarbans have breathing roots poking up like pencils.
terms.art: Muddy ground at low tide with hundreds of pencil-like roots poking up around a mangrove tree.

terms.meaning: The wide, flat part of a leaf.
terms.example: A banana leaf has a huge blade. A pine needle has a very thin one.
terms.art: A big banana leaf and a pine needle side by side, with the blades shaded.

terms.meaning: The thin lines in a leaf. They carry water in and food out, and they hold the leaf open like the spokes of an umbrella.
terms.example: Hold a leaf up to the window. You can see its veins.
terms.art: A leaf held up against a bright window, its veins glowing like a map of rivers.

terms.meaning: A tiny hole in a leaf's skin, too small to see without a microscope. Air goes in and water vapour comes out through it.
terms.example: One leaf can have many thousands of stomata.
terms.art: A zoom into a leaf's skin showing tiny mouth-like holes, each between two bean-shaped cells.

terms.meaning: The green substance in leaves. It catches sunlight so the leaf can make food.
terms.example: Chlorophyll is why leaves, grass and peas are green.
terms.art: A leaf zooming in to tiny green blobs inside its cells.

terms.meaning: A hard, sharp point on a plant. A cactus's spines are leaves that have changed shape.
terms.example: Touch a cactus gently and you feel its spines.
terms.art: A close-up of cactus spines growing from little cushions on a green stem.

terms.meaning: The tiny building block that every living thing is made of. A leaf is built from millions of cells.
terms.example: Onion skin under a microscope looks like a wall of tiny bricks. Each brick is a cell.
terms.art: A thin onion skin under a microscope, showing rows of brick-shaped cells.

terms.meaning: A scientist who studies plants.
terms.example: Janaki Ammal was an Indian botanist who studied sugarcane.
terms.art: A botanist kneeling in a field with a notebook and a magnifying glass.

explanations.concept: Every part has a job, and the parts need each other
explanations.definition: Most plants have roots, a stem and leaves. Many also have flowers, which make fruits and seeds. Each part has its own job, and the parts need each other. A cut-off part lives on only if it can grow the parts it is missing, as a money plant cutting grows new roots in a glass of water.
explanations.description: The roots hold on and soak up water. The stem holds everything up and carries water and food between the roots and the leaves. The leaves catch sunlight and make food. The flowers make seeds, and the fruits protect the seeds and help spread them. Botanists, the scientists who study plants, split the plant into two halves. Everything under the ground is the root system. Everything above the ground is the shoot system. The roots need food from the leaves. The leaves need water from the roots. So each part depends on the others.
examples: Cut a rose and put it in a vase. Without roots it lasts only a few days.
Cover every leaf of a plant and they slowly starve, even with plenty of water.
In a coriander bunch from the market, you can see roots, stems and leaves on one small plant.
explanations.art: A coriander plant laid on white paper, with roots, stem and leaves labelled and arrows showing water going up and food going down.
explanations.context: This card is about the main idea you met in earlier classes: a plant has parts, and each part has a job.

explanations.definition: The shape of each plant part helps it do its job. Scientists say form fits function. Form means shape, and function means job.
explanations.description: Look at the parts of any plant and ask, 'Why this shape?' A root is long and thin and branches again and again, so it can reach water far away and grip lots of soil. A leaf is thin and flat, so it can spread out to catch light. A tree trunk is thick and round, so it can stand up to wind from any side. Here is the surprise. Plants that are not related at all often end up with the same shapes when they live in the same kind of place. Cactuses in America and some euphorbias in Africa look almost the same. Both are fat, green and spiny. But they come from different plant families. Each family came to this shape on its own, because the same shape works in the same kind of place.
examples: A lotus leaf is round and flat, so it floats like a plate.
A pine needle is thin and tough, so it loses little water in cold, dry winds.
A bean stem is thin and bendy, so it can wind round a stick.
explanations.art: Two look-alike spiny green plants side by side, one labelled America, one labelled Africa, with different family trees behind them.
explanations.context: This card is the big idea of the whole unit. Every shape in a plant is there for a reason.

explanations.concept: Roots: holding on and soaking up water
explanations.definition: Roots hold the plant in the ground and soak up water and minerals from the soil. Some plants have one big tap root. Others have a bunch of thin fibrous roots.
explanations.description: A tap root is one thick main root that grows straight down, like a tent peg. It can reach deep water and hold a plant firm. Fibrous roots are a beard of thin roots near the top of the soil. They grip the soil like a net and catch rain quickly. Just behind the tip of each young root are root hairs, far thinner than the hairs on your head. They push between the soil grains and soak up water. Roots are thin and many because a thin root can squeeze between soil grains, and many roots touch far more soil than one fat root could. In 1937 a scientist called Howard Dittmer grew one rye plant in a box of soil for four months. Then he washed out and measured their roots. Together they were about 600 kilometres long. The root hairs added more than 10,000 kilometres. The unit on how water travels through a plant follows the water from these hairs up to the leaves.
examples: Mustard, neem and carrot have tap roots.
Grass, wheat, rice and onion have fibrous roots.
In the Kalahari Desert in Africa, roots of a shepherd's tree have been found about 68 metres down. That is deeper than a 20-storey building is tall.
explanations.art: Two plants with the soil cut away: a mustard plant with one deep tap root, and a grass tuft with a wide beard of fibrous roots, with a magnified circle showing root hairs between soil grains.
explanations.context: Roots are hidden, so we forget about them. This card shows why roots are shaped the way they are.

explanations.definition: Some roots grow fat because they are full of stored food. The food was made in the leaves and sent down the stem to be kept for later.
explanations.description: A carrot, a radish, a beetroot and a sweet potato are all storage roots. They taste sweet or starchy because they are packed with food. But the plant did not store that food for us. They stored it for their own use. A carrot's life has two parts. First they grow leaves and fill their root with sugar. Then, after the cold weather, they use that stored food very fast. They send up a tall stalk with white umbrella-shaped flowers, and makes seeds. In cold countries this takes two years. In north India it happens between autumn and the next spring. Farmers in north India use this. They dig up their carrots in winter, choose the best ones and plant them again. By spring those carrots have flowered and made seed for next year. If you dig up a carrot after they have flowered, the root is woody and not sweet. Their food has gone up into the flowers and seeds.
examples: A carrot top left in a saucer of water grows new leaves, using food stored at its top.
Sweet potato, shakarkand, is a root, even though a potato is a stem.
Beetroot is so full of sugar that a kind of beet, called sugar beet, is grown in many cold countries to make sugar.
explanations.art: A carrot plant in two panels: first, leafy with a fat orange root, and later, a tall stalk of white umbrella flowers and a thin woody root.
explanations.context: Why are carrots and radishes so fat? This card explains what a fat root is for, and who it is really for.

explanations.definition: Roots can do more than hold on and drink. Some roots prop the plant up like pillars. Some breathe. Some climb. Some even grow into living bridges.
explanations.description: A banyan tree sends down thin roots from their branches. When they reach the ground, they grow thick and woody, like pillars. These prop roots hold up the huge branches, so the tree can spread wider and wider. Mangrove trees grow in salty mud by the sea, where there is almost no air in the soil. Their breathing roots poke up out of the mud like pencils, and air gets in through tiny holes. A money plant and a paan creeper climb walls with short roots that grow out of their stems and grip like fingers. Orchids hang on trees with spongy roots that soak up rain from the air. In Meghalaya, Khasi and Jaintia people guide the aerial roots of rubber fig trees across streams. Over many years the roots grow thick, join together and become bridges strong enough for people to walk on.
examples: The Great Banyan in the botanic garden at Howrah, near Kolkata, stands on more than 3,000 pillar roots.
Maize and sugarcane grow short prop roots near the ground, like tent pegs.
In the Sundarbans, mangrove breathing roots stick up out of the mud at low tide.
explanations.art: Four small scenes: a banyan's pillar roots, mangrove breathing roots in mud, a money plant gripping a wall, and a living root bridge over a stream in a misty forest.
explanations.context: Roots are not always underground. This card shows roots that hold up trees, breathe, climb and even make bridges.

explanations.concept: Stems: holding the plant up and carrying water and food
explanations.definition: A stem holds the leaves up to the light and the flowers up to the insects. Inside, tiny tubes carry water up from the roots and food from the leaves to the rest of the plant.
explanations.description: A stem's shape depends on how much it has to hold up. A herb, like coriander, has a soft green stem because it holds up only a few leaves. A tree has a thick woody trunk, because they must hold up a huge crown against wind and rain. Many stems are tubes. Bamboo and wheat stems are hollow tubes. At each ring, called a node, a solid wall runs across the inside of the tube, and this stops the tube from squashing flat when it bends. A tube is very strong for its weight. People make poles and bicycle frames from tubes for the same reason. Not every stem is hollow. Sugarcane is filled with soft, juicy tissue that stores sugar. Stems also have nodes, the places where leaves and buds grow. That is how botanists tell a stem from a root, even under the ground. Stems have nodes and buds. Roots usually do not.
examples: Bamboo is a giant grass with a hollow stem, so strong that it is used for scaffolding.
The rings on sugarcane are nodes, where leaves once grew.
A tree trunk grows thicker every year, so it can hold up more branches.
explanations.art: A bamboo pole cut open to show it is hollow, next to a bicycle frame made of tubes, with a coriander stalk for comparison.
explanations.context: This card is about the stem, the part that holds a plant up. It shows why so many stems are shaped like tubes.

explanations.definition: Some stems grow fat and store food, often under the ground. Potato, ginger, turmeric, chembu and sugarcane all store food in their stems.
explanations.description: A potato looks like a root, but it is a stem. You can tell from its eyes. Each eye is a bud, and the eyes sit in a spiral round the potato, just as leaves sit in a spiral round a stem. Ginger and turmeric are stems that grow sideways under the ground. Look for the rings on them. Those are nodes. Chembu is a short, fat underground stem. Sugarcane stores sugar in their tall stem above the ground. An onion is a little different. Its bottom is a tiny flat stem, and its juicy layers are swollen leaves full of stored food. So the onion stores food in its leaves. Plants store food in underground stems so they can survive a dry season or a cold winter, and grow again quickly when the rain comes.
examples: Farmers cut seed potatoes into pieces, making sure each piece has at least one eye. Each eye can grow a new plant.
A piece of ginger left in a damp place grows a green shoot from one of its buds.
Sugarcane is crushed to get its sweet juice, which is made into jaggery and sugar.
explanations.art: A kitchen board with a potato showing its eyes in a spiral, a ginger piece with its rings, a sugarcane piece with nodes, and a halved onion with its layers.
explanations.context: Some of the food we eat is stored in stems. This card shows which ones, and how to spot a stem when it looks like a root.

explanations.definition: A climber is a plant with a thin stem that reaches the light by holding on to something else. Some climbers twine round a support. Others grab with tendrils, hook on with thorns or cling with roots.
explanations.description: Plants need light to make their food. In a crowded garden or forest, the tallest plants get the most light. A tree reaches the light by building a thick trunk, which takes years. A climber grows a thin stem that needs much less food to build, and they lean on something else. A twiner, like a bean, winds their whole stem round a stick. A pea or a gourd sends out tendrils, curly threads that coil round anything they touch. Bougainvillea hooks on with thorns. A money plant clings with little roots. A young climbing shoot does not grow straight. Its tip slowly sweeps round in circles, feeling for something to hold. Charles Darwin timed a hop shoot. One full circle took about two hours. He also found that some tendrils start to curl within a minute or two of a touch.
examples: Scientists counted the twining plants of the world. About 9 out of every 10 kinds wind the same way.
Hops and honeysuckle are famous for twisting the other way.
Amarbel, called dodder, is a twining plant with no proper leaves. They feed on other plants, and as a seedling they find them by smell.
explanations.art: A bean twining up a stick, a gourd tendril coiled round a string, bougainvillea thorns hooked on a wall and money-plant roots gripping a pole.
explanations.context: Why do some plants climb instead of standing up by themselves? This card explains how climbers reach the light without building a trunk.

explanations.definition: When a tendril grabs a support, it coils into a spring that twists one way at one end and the other way at the other end. In the middle there is a switch point.
explanations.description: Once the tip of a tendril has caught hold, both of its ends are fixed. One end is on the plant and one end is on the support. A thread fixed at both ends cannot coil all one way without twisting itself up. So it coils one way for part of its length and the other way for the rest, and the two twists cancel out. Darwin saw this switch point and described it. In 2012, a team of scientists at Harvard University worked out exactly how it happens. One side of the tendril shrinks more than the other, so it curls. The spring shape pulls the plant closer to their support, and lets them stretch a little in the wind without snapping.
examples: An old curly telephone cord often has a switch point where the twist changes direction.
A coiled gourd tendril pulls the vine up towards the string it caught.
explanations.art: A close-up of a coiled gourd tendril, with arrows showing the twist going one way, a switch point in the middle, then the twist going the other way.
explanations.context: Tendrils are the curly threads that climbing plants use to grab things. This card is about a strange twist in every coiled tendril.

explanations.definition: Most leaves are thin, flat and wide. This shape spreads them out to catch as much sunlight as possible.
explanations.description: A leaf works like a solar panel. A wide, flat shape catches lots of light. A thin leaf lets the light and air reach every cell inside it. The veins hold the leaf open, like the spokes of an umbrella. Leaves are also arranged so they do not shade each other. Look down on a plant from above. The leaves fit together like a jigsaw, with few gaps and few overlaps. Many plants grow their leaves in a spiral round the stem, each one turned a little from the last, so every leaf gets its own patch of sky. Leaves even change shape with the light. Leaves in the shade grow bigger and thinner, to catch every bit of weak light. Leaves in full sun are smaller and thicker. The unit on photosynthesis explains what the leaf does with the light it catches.
examples: Shade plants, like the money plant on a dim landing, often have big, thin leaves.
In a field of grown sunflowers, almost every flower head faces east, towards the morning Sun.
Look down on a tulsi plant. Each pair of leaves sits at right angles to the pair below.
explanations.art: A view from above a plant, their leaves fitting together like a jigsaw, and a sun leaf and a shade leaf from the same bush side by side.
explanations.context: Leaves come in many shapes, but most are thin and flat. This card explains why, and how leaves avoid shading each other.

chart.title: Made-up example: size of sun leaves and shade leaves from one hibiscus bush
chart.y: Leaf size (squares covered on 1 cm squared paper)
chart.note: These numbers are made up. Your leaves will give different numbers.

explanations.definition: Where light, water or food is hard to get, leaves change shape. Some become spines, some float, some store water and some even catch insects.
explanations.description: In a desert, a wide leaf would lose too much water. So a cactus has no wide leaves. Their leaves have become spines that guard them, and their fat green stem does the leaf's job. Aloe stores water in thick, juicy leaves. On a pond, a lotus leaf is round and flat, so it floats. Its tiny holes, the stomata, are on the top side, facing the air, not underneath in the water. Its skin is covered with tiny waxy bumps, so water rolls off in balls and carries the dirt away. Scientists call this the lotus effect. In the Amazon, a giant water lily grows leaves wider than a car, held up by thick ribs underneath. A garden designer called Joseph Paxton said those ribs gave him the idea for a huge glass building in London, the Crystal Palace, in 1851. In Meghalaya, a pitcher plant grows in poor soil. Their leaves end in jugs that trap insects, which feed them.
examples: Pine trees in cold mountains have needle leaves that lose little water.
Chembu (arbi) leaves, like lotus leaves, make raindrops roll off in shiny balls.
Jalkumbhi, water hyacinth, has puffy leaf stalks full of air, so they float on ponds.
explanations.art: Five panels: a cactus with spines, a lotus leaf with water beads, a giant water lily leaf with a small child sitting on it, a pitcher plant jug, and a pine needle.
explanations.context: Not every leaf is thin and flat. This card shows leaves that changed shape to live in deserts, ponds and poor soil.

explanations.concept: Is every part secretly a leaf?
explanations.description: About 230 years ago, a German poet and thinker had a bold idea. He said that petals, tendrils, spines and many other parts above the ground are all leaves that have changed shape. Botanists have argued about how far this idea goes ever since. Some parts really are changed leaves. Others are not. And for some, like a gourd's tendril, botanists still disagree.
examples: A pea's tendrils are the tips of their leaves. You can see them growing where the last leaflets should be.
A cactus spine is a changed leaf.
Bougainvillea's thorns are changed branches, not leaves. So not every part is a leaf.

perspectives.who: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe, a German poet and thinker, in 1790
perspectives.explanation: In a book called The Metamorphosis of Plants, he said every part above the ground, even the parts of a flower, is the same basic leaf in a different form.

perspectives.who: Agnes Arber, an English botanist, in 1950
perspectives.explanation: She studied plant shapes for fifty years, much of it in a small laboratory in her own home. She argued that a leaf is really a 'part of a shoot' that stopped growing early. She was the first woman botanist chosen as a member of Britain's top science society, the Royal Society, in 1946.

Enrico Coen and Elliot Meyerowitz found the genes that turn a leaf into each part of a flower. When those genes are switched off, a flower grows only leaf-like parts. So Goethe was partly right about flowers. But other parts, like many thorns, come from stems.

explanations.art: A row of plant parts, petal, tendril, spine and pitcher, each with a dotted line leading back to an ordinary leaf, and a question mark over a gourd tendril.
explanations.context: Plants have many strange parts: spines, tendrils, petals, pitchers. This card is about an old question. Are they all leaves in disguise?

explanations.concept: Inside a leaf: cells, chlorophyll and packets of light
explanations.description: Zoom into a leaf and you find millions of cells, packed like bricks. Inside each cell are tiny green blobs full of chlorophyll. Keep zooming. Each chlorophyll molecule is a ring of atoms with one magnesium atom at its centre. Light is made of tiny packets of energy called photons. When a photon hits a chlorophyll molecule, its energy is caught and passed along, from molecule to molecule, to the place where food is made. All of that is agreed. Scientists argue about one part. How does the energy find its way so fast, and lose so little on the way?
examples: A leaf is only a few cells thick, so light can reach the green blobs in almost every cell.
Chlorophyll catches red and blue light best. It catches less green light, so more green bounces back to our eyes.

perspectives.who: Gregory Engel, Graham Fleming and colleagues, in America, in 2007
perspectives.explanation: In the light-catching parts of some bacteria, the energy seemed to behave like a wave. It seemed to spread along many paths at once, instead of hopping along one path. This is an idea from quantum physics, the science of the very tiny.
Repeating the tests in conditions more like real sunlight, some found the wave effect fades far too quickly to matter much. The question is still argued about.

explanations.art: A zoom in four steps: a leaf, cells like green bricks, green blobs inside a cell, and a ring-shaped chlorophyll molecule catching a tiny glowing photon.
explanations.context: This card zooms far inside a leaf, down to atoms and packets of light. It shows how a leaf really catches sunlight.

explanations.concept: Why are leaves green and not black?
explanations.description: This sounds like a silly question, but it is a real puzzle. A black leaf would soak up every colour of light. A green leaf still soaks up most of the green light, but it lets more green bounce off than red or blue. Green is one of the strongest parts of sunlight. So why are almost all leaves green? Nobody is completely sure. In 2020, Nathaniel Gabor and his team in California suggested an idea. Sunlight flickers up and down as clouds and leaves move. A leaf may be tuned to catch light steadily, without being flooded when the Sun bursts out. Letting some green go may keep the leaf's light-catcher running smoothly, like a car that avoids sudden speeding up and braking. Other scientists think plants are green simply because of the history of life. Their ancestors in the sea used this kind of chlorophyll, and plants never switched.
examples: Some leaves look red or purple, like red amaranth, lal saag. They still have chlorophyll, hidden by red colours.
Sunlight is strongest in the blue-green and green part of the rainbow.

perspectives.explanation: Leaves let some green light go to keep their energy supply steady when the light keeps changing.
Leaves are green because their ancient ancestors in the sea were built that way, and changing would be too hard. Both ideas may be partly true.

explanations.art: A green leaf and an imaginary black leaf side by side under the Sun, with rainbow arrows bouncing off the green leaf.
explanations.context: Nearly every leaf in the world is green. This card is about a surprise: scientists are still not sure why.

explanations.concept: How plants grew their parts: a story 470 million years long
explanations.definition: The first plants on land had no roots and no leaves. Over many millions of years, plants grew roots, then woody stems, then wide leaves, and much later flowers.
explanations.description: For about three billion years, almost all life lived in water. Then, about 470 million years ago, small green plants began to live on land. Fossils show that some of the earliest, like Cooksonia, were just thin forked stems, shorter than your finger, with no roots and no leaves. In rocks at Rhynie in Scotland, about 407 million years old, scientists found whole little plants turned to stone. They had no true roots. By about 400 million years ago, plants had roots and woody stems. By about 385 million years ago there were the first forests of real trees. Wide flat leaves only became common later, about 360 million years ago. Flowering plants came last, about 130 million years ago. Why did wide leaves take so long? One idea, from David Beerling and colleagues, is about the air. Early air had much more carbon dioxide, so leaves needed only a few stomata to take it in. Leaves cool down by letting water out through their stomata. With so few stomata, a wide leaf in the sun would have overheated. That idea is still being tested.
examples: Roots changed the whole Earth. They cracked rocks and helped make the first deep soils.
Much of India's coal formed from forests of plants that grew about 250 to 300 million years ago.
explanations.art: A timeline from left to right: a tiny forked stem with no leaves, a plant with roots, a first forest of tall trees, wide leaves, and finally a flower.
explanations.context: Plants did not always have roots, stems and leaves. This card tells how plants built their parts, one at a time, over hundreds of millions of years.

explanations.description: If there are plants on planets around other stars, what would they look like? Their leaves would be shaped by the light they get, just like leaves on Earth. Nancy Kiang, a scientist at NASA, worked on this with her team. Many stars are smaller and redder than our Sun. On a planet circling a red star, the light is dim and reddish. Plants there might be dark, even black, to catch every bit of it. On a planet with a brighter, bluer star, plants might reflect more light and look yellow or orange. Nobody has found plants on another planet. This is a careful guess, based on the rules that shape leaves here.
examples: Our Sun is a yellow-white star. A lot of its light reaches the ground as the colours we can see.
Most stars in our galaxy are small red stars, and many planets have been found circling them.
explanations.art: Three imaginary planets with different coloured stars in their skies: one with green plants, one with nearly black plants under a red star, one with orange plants under a blue-white star.
explanations.context: Leaves are shaped by the light they catch. This card imagines what plants might look like on planets around other stars.

agreed.text: Each part of a plant has a job, and its shape helps it do that job.
agreed.evidence: Botanists have compared thousands of plants. Plants that live in the same kind of place often grow the same shapes, even when they are not related.

agreed.text: Some roots and stems store food for the plant to use later.
agreed.evidence: Povidone-iodine, a brown liquid from the chemist, turns blue-black on a cut potato. That shows stored starch. A carrot top in water grows new leaves with no soil, using its stored food.

agreed.text: You can tell a stem from a root by its nodes and buds.
agreed.evidence: A potato's eyes grow into shoots. Ginger and sugarcane have rings where leaves once grew. Most roots have no buds like these.

agreed.text: Climbing plants sense touch and move to hold on.
agreed.evidence: Charles Darwin timed tendrils curling after a touch, and drew the circles made by growing shoot tips. Anyone can repeat these tests with a gourd or pea plant.

agreed.text: Leaves are arranged and shaped to catch light.
agreed.evidence: Photos taken from above plants show leaves fitting together like a jigsaw. Leaves grown in shade are bigger and thinner than leaves grown in sun on the same plant.

agreed.text: The first land plants had no roots or leaves.
agreed.evidence: Fossils of the oldest land plants, such as those in the 407-million-year-old rocks at Rhynie in Scotland, show small stems without true roots or leaves.

challenging.claim: Potatoes and carrots are both roots, because they both grow under the ground.
challenging.who: Many people, and some picture books
challenging.for: Both grow in the soil, both are fat, and both are dug up.
challenging.against: A potato has eyes, which are buds, and buds grow on stems. Put an old potato in a dark basket and its eyes sprout shoots. A carrot has no eyes along its sides. Where a part grows does not tell you what it is. Its clues do.
challenging.context: This card is about a very common mix-up between two vegetables found in every Indian kitchen.

challenging.claim: Plants are simple, because they cannot move.
challenging.for: Plants have no muscles and no brain. They stay in one place all their lives.
challenging.against: Plants move, just slowly. Shoot tips sweep round in circles. Tendrils coil round a stick within hours, sometimes minutes. Leaves turn to face the light. Speed up a film of a growing bean and they look like they are searching.
challenging.context: This card asks whether plants are as still and simple as they look.

challenging.claim: Fat roots grow big so that people and animals can eat them.
challenging.who: A way of thinking many of us have without noticing
challenging.for: We grow carrots and radishes for food, and farmers choose the biggest ones.
challenging.against: The root stores food for the plant's own future. A carrot left in the ground uses their stored sugar to grow a tall flower stalk and seeds. People did breed carrots to be bigger and sweeter, but the store was there first, for the plant.
challenging.context: Carrots and beetroots are fat and sweet. This card asks who that food is really for.

challenging.who: Almost everyone, in songs and sayings
challenging.for: They are sharp and pointed, like thorns.
challenging.against: Botanists say a true thorn is a changed branch, like bougainvillea's. A rose's sharp points grow only from their skin. You can snap one off cleanly, and there is no bud near it. Botanists call them prickles. In everyday speech, though, nobody minds if you call them thorns.
challenging.context: This card is about the sharp points on rose stems, and what botanists call them.

challenging.claim: Charles Darwin was the first person to study how plants climb.
challenging.for: Darwin wrote a famous book on climbing plants, in 1875, and did many clever experiments.
challenging.against: In 1827, two German botanists, Hugo von Mohl and Ludwig Palm, each wrote books about how climbing plants twine and grab. Darwin read them and named them in his own work. Famous names often stand on the work of people we forget.
challenging.context: This card is about who gets the credit for discovering how climbing plants work.

challenging.claim: Leaves are green because green is the best colour for catching sunlight.
challenging.for: Leaves are so good at catching light that their colour must be the best one.
challenging.against: A leaf looks green because it lets more green light bounce off than red or blue. Black would catch more light. Why leaves let some green go is still being studied.
challenging.context: Leaves catch light to make food. This card is about whether their green colour helps or not.

big_questions.q: A carrot fills their root with sugar, then uses it all to make flowers and seeds. Why might a plant save food first and spend it later?
big_questions.hint: Think about winter, or a dry season, when the leaves cannot make much food.

big_questions.q: A climber grows a thin stem and leans on other plants. What do they gain, and what do they risk?
big_questions.hint: Think about the food they save, and what happens to the bean with no stick.

big_questions.q: Roots are hidden, so we hardly see them. Could a plant have more of their body under the ground than above it?
big_questions.hint: One rye plant's roots, laid end to end, were about 600 kilometres long.

big_questions.q: If every part of a plant is shaped for its job, what is your hand shaped for? What about your ear, or your eye?
big_questions.hint: Open and close your hand. Count the jobs it can do.

big_questions.q: Plants that are not related grow the same shapes when they live in the same kind of place. Does the place shape the living thing?
big_questions.hint: Think of cactuses in America and spiny euphorbias in Africa. They are not related, but they look almost the same.

big_questions.q: Is a potato a root because it grows underground, or a stem because it has buds? Who decides what a thing is?
big_questions.hint: What clues would you trust more: where something is, or what it does and how it is built?

big_questions.q: Why are leaves green and not black, when black would catch more light?
big_questions.hint: Scientists are still not sure. What would happen to a solar panel if the Sun kept bursting out from behind clouds?

big_questions.q: The first land plants had no roots and no leaves. What do you think the land looked like then?
big_questions.hint: No grass, no trees, no soil as we know it. Just rock, water and tiny green stems.

big_questions.q: A root bridge gets stronger every year, while a bridge of cut bamboo slowly rots. What is different about a bridge that is alive?
big_questions.hint: A living root keeps growing. Cut bamboo cannot grow or mend itself.

big_questions.q: If there are plants on a planet with a red star, would they still be 'plants' if they were black?
big_questions.hint: What makes a plant a plant: their colour, or their job?

big_questions.q: A tendril coils as soon as it is touched. Does a plant feel? What would count as feeling?
big_questions.hint: The unit on plant senses looks at this question. What do you think feeling needs?

story.title: Ten Carrots for Next Year
story.note: Jasmeet, her family and their village are made up. The farming is real. In north India, farmers grow carrot seed by digging up the best carrots in winter and planting them again. This is called the root-to-seed method.
text: In the village of Kheri, near Karnal, the winter fog sat on the fields like a grey quilt. Under the fog, under the soil, the carrots were growing fat and red.

Jasmeet was nine, and she loved carrots more than anything. She loved them raw, with a pinch of salt. She loved them in gajar halwa, glossy with ghee. Most of all, she loved pulling one out of the cold ground with both hands and hearing the soft pop they made as they let go.
This year, her father had gone to work in a dhaba in Chandigarh for the winter. So it was Jasmeet and her mother, Harpreet, who would harvest the field.

In the corner of the kitchen stood the old steel tin where the family kept its carrot seed. Every year, a handful of seed from that tin became a whole field. But in January, a heavy winter rain had dripped through a crack in the roof, straight into the tin. When Harpreet opened it, the seeds were black and furry with mould. She closed the lid very quietly.
'We will buy seed from the shop next year,' she said. But Jasmeet had seen her face. Shop seed came in shiny packets, and it cost a great deal of money.

Harvest day came. Mother and daughter worked down the rows, pulling, shaking off soil, twisting off the leafy tops. The baskets filled with red. Some carrots were thin and forked, like a man with two legs. Some were fat and straight and as long as Jasmeet's forearm.
'The fat ones fetch the best price at the mandi,' said Harpreet. 'Put those on top.'
Jasmeet held a fat one up to the pale Sun. It was so heavy for its size. So sweet. Why does a carrot make themselves so sweet? she wondered. It is not as if they want to be eaten.
Then she remembered something.

Last spring, at the far edge of the field, behind the tube well, one carrot had been missed. Nobody had pulled them. In February their feathery leaves had grown thick. In March a stalk had shot up out of the middle, taller than Jasmeet herself, and at the top it had opened into white flowers. They were like umbrellas made of tiny stars. Bees had crawled over them all day long, humming. Later the umbrellas had dried and curled shut like fists. When Jasmeet shook one, little brown seeds had fallen into her palm.
She had pulled up that carrot, out of curiosity, in April. It was no longer red and sweet. It was pale and hard, like a stick of wood. She had wondered where all its sweetness had gone.
Now, standing in the field with the fat carrot in her hand, she knew.

The sweetness had gone up. Up the stalk, into the umbrellas, into the seeds. The carrot had not been storing their sugar for her. They had been packing their own lunch, for their own journey. They needed that food to grow a stalk taller than a girl, and a hundred flowers, and a thousand seeds, all in one spring.
'Mummy,' she said. 'Don't sell all of them.'
Harpreet looked up, tired. 'Jassi, every fat carrot is money.'
'Ten,' said Jasmeet. 'Just the ten best. We plant them again, at the edge of the field. They will flower. And then we will have seed. Our own seed, like before.'

Her mother frowned. 'Plant carrots that are already grown? Who does that?' But Jasmeet told her about the carrot behind the tube well, the stalk, the bees, the seeds and the woody root. She told it all in one breath.
Harpreet was quiet for a while. Then she picked up the fattest carrot and turned it over in her hands, as if she was seeing it for the first time.

'Your nani used to do something like this,' she said slowly. 'I was too small to understand.' Then she gave Jasmeet a small knife and showed her how to trim the leaves, leaving a crown of green at the top. 'Not too close,' she said. 'The new shoot grows from there.'

They chose ten. Straight ones, red to the core, with no cracks. Jasmeet planted them in a row by the tube well, each one in their own hole, the green crown just peeping out of the soil. She pressed the earth round each one as gently as if she was tucking them into bed. The rest of the carrots went to the mandi.

For two weeks, nothing seemed to happen. Then the crowns pushed out new leaves, fresh and feathery. By March, ten stalks were rising, one from each carrot. They grew so fast that Jasmeet measured them against her own body every morning. Knee. Waist. Shoulder.

Then the umbrellas opened. Ten plants, and on each one a hundred little white umbrellas, and on each umbrella a hundred tiny stars. The bees came from everywhere. The edge of the field hummed like a temple bell long after it has been struck.

In April the umbrellas dried and curled up into brown nests. Jasmeet and her mother cut them carefully into a cloth, and rubbed them between their palms. The seeds fell out, small and brown and smelling faintly of carrot. There were so many that they filled the old steel tin almost to the top.
That evening, Jasmeet dug up one of the ten carrots. It was pale and woody, exactly like the one from last year. She held it next to the full tin of seed.
When her father came home for Baisakhi, she showed him both. She did not explain. She just put the woody carrot in one of his hands and the tin of seed in the other, and watched him understand.
story.epiphany: For the parent: a carrot is a storage root. The plant packs it with sugar made by their leaves, not for us but for their own next stage, when they use that food to grow a tall flower stalk and seeds. Jasmeet's turn comes when she connects the sweet root with the woody root she found after the forgotten carrot flowered. The sweetness had moved up into the flowers and seeds. Shape and job go together: the root is fat because its job is to store. The story also quietly asks who seeds belong to, and what we keep back for the future.
ask: Why do you think a carrot makes themselves so sweet, if they do not want to be eaten?
Where did the sweetness of the forgotten carrot go?
Why did Harpreet leave a crown of green at the top of each carrot?
Jasmeet's mother wanted to sell every fat carrot. Jasmeet wanted to keep ten. Who was right, and why?
Jasmeet chose straight carrots with no cracks. Why choose the best carrots to make seed?

games.title: Plant Part Disguises
games.players: 2 to 5 players, or one child playing against the app

printables.title: 24 disguise cards to cut out (the answer is on the back)

items.f: Carrot: fat and orange, under the ground
Potato: has eyes that sprout in a dark basket
Ginger: knobbly, with rings, grows sideways underground
Onion: made of juicy layers on a flat bottom
Sugarcane: tall and sweet, with rings
Radish (mullangi): long, white, under the ground, with no eyes
Pea tendril: curly thread at the end of a leaf
Cactus spine: sharp point on a desert plant
Cactus pad: fat, green and juicy, with spines
Banyan pillar: hangs down from a branch, then grows thick
Mangrove pencil: pokes up out of salty mud
Money plant grip: little brown fingers clinging to a wall
Bean spiral: winds round and round a stick
Bougainvillea hook: sharp and woody, near a bud
Lotus plate: round, flat and floating
Pitcher jug: a trap full of water that catches insects
Aloe: thick, juicy and full of water
Turmeric: orange inside, with rings, underground
Sweet potato: fat and sweet, underground
Chembu: round, hairy, underground, with a bud on top
TEST IT: find a potato in the kitchen. Count its eyes.
items.b: A potato is a STEM. The eyes of a potato are buds.

items.f: TEST IT: peel one layer of an onion. Is it like a leaf?
items.b: Yes. The layers of an onion are leaves.

items.f: TEST IT: look down on a pot plant from above. Do the leaves overlap much?
items.b: Look and see. Leaves grow in different places so each one can catch light.

items.f: TEST IT: hold a leaf up to the window. Find its veins.
items.b: Veins are the thin lines that carry water and food.

rules: Cut out the 24 cards. Shuffle them and put them face down in a pile.
On your turn, take the top card and read it out loud.
Decide what the part really is: a root, a stem or a leaf in disguise. Put it in that column on the mat. Then turn the card over to check.
Then pick the job token that fits: stores food, climbs, catches light, holds on, protects, stores water or breathes. Say how the shape helps with that job. A good reason wins the card.
If you draw a TEST IT card, everyone does the test. The first person to explain the result wins two cards.
When the pile runs out, the player with the most cards wins.

flow.do: 1. Lay the mat on the floor with its three columns: ROOT, STEM and LEAF. 2. Shuffle the 24 cards and put them face down. 3. Put the job tokens in a bowl.
flow.say: Every card is a plant part in disguise. It might look like a root, but be a stem. Or look like a thread, but be a leaf. Your job is to see through the disguise.
flow.kid: Put the mat down: ROOT, STEM, LEAF. Mix the cards and put them face down. Each card is a plant part in disguise. Can you see through it?
flow.context: This is the first step of Plant Part Disguises. It is a card game about plant parts that have changed shape for a special job.

flow.do: Find the potato card. Play it together as a practice round.
flow.say: Let's practise. 'Potato: has eyes that sprout in a dark basket.' Root, stem or leaf?
flow.kid: Practice card: the potato. It has eyes that sprout. Root, stem or leaf? Tap your answer.

ask.q: What clue tells you the potato is a stem?
good: Its eyes are buds, and buds grow on stems.

check.q: A potato has eyes that sprout. What is a potato really?
options: A root
A stem
A leaf
check.why: A potato's eyes are buds, and buds grow on stems. Each eye can sprout a new shoot. So a potato is a fat underground stem, called a tuber. Picking 'root' usually means deciding by where it grows. Lots of stems grow under the ground.

flow.do: 1. Take turns. Each player draws a card, reads it and puts it in a column. 2. They choose a job token and say how the shape helps. 3. Others agree or argue. A good reason wins the card.
flow.say: When you put a card down, tell us its job. Then tell us how its shape helps it do that job.
flow.kid: Take turns. Read your card. Put it under ROOT, STEM or LEAF. Pick a job token. Say how the shape helps.
flow.parent: Answers to expect. Roots: carrot, radish, sweet potato, banyan pillar, mangrove pencil, money plant grip. Stems: potato, ginger, turmeric, sugarcane, chembu, cactus pad, bean spiral, bougainvillea hook. Leaves: onion layers, pea tendril, cactus spine, lotus plate, pitcher jug, aloe. A good reason links the shape to the job. For example, 'The pencil roots stick up out of the mud so air can get in.'

flow.do: When a TEST IT card comes up, stop and do it together. Everyone guesses first.
flow.say: Before we test it, everyone guess. Then let's look and see who was right.
flow.kid: A TEST IT card! Guess first. Then do the test. Were you right?

ask.q: You peeled an onion layer. Why is it a leaf?
good: It is thin and grows from the flat stem at the bottom, like leaves grow from a stem.
The green tops of a spring onion join on to the layers.

flow.think: Why would a plant store food in their leaves, under the ground?

flow.do: Count the cards to find the winner. Then look at the three columns together.
flow.say: Look at the three columns. Which part changes its shape most often?
flow.kid: Count your cards. Who won? Look at the columns. Which part wears the most disguises?
flow.think: If parts can change shape so much, how do botanists ever tell what they are?

games.context: This is a card game about plant parts in disguise. Players decide whether each strange part is really a root, a stem or a leaf, and say what its shape is for.

games.title: Build a Plant to Survive

printables.title: 6 place cards
items: Hot desert: rain once a year
Dark forest floor under tall trees
Salty mud by the sea, flooded twice a day
Crowded garden, everyone fighting for light

printables.title: 18 part cards
items: ROOT: long tap root that reaches deep water
ROOT: wide fibrous roots that catch rain fast
ROOT: pillar roots that hold up branches
ROOT: breathing roots that poke out of mud
ROOT: clinging roots that grip walls
STEM: fat green stem that stores water
STEM: underground stem that stores food
LEAF: round floating leaf with a waxy top

printables.title: 8 trouble cards
items: A goat comes to eat you
A tall tree grows and shades you
The soil has almost no food

rules: Each player takes a place card. That is where your plant must live.
Lay the 18 part cards face up. Take turns choosing one root, one stem and one leaf for your plant.
Draw your plant on the survival sheet and give them a name.
Then take a trouble card. Explain how your plant's parts help them survive the trouble. The others vote: did they survive?
A surviving plant scores one point for each part that helped. Play three rounds with new trouble cards.

flow.do: 1. Give each player a place card. 2. Lay the 18 part cards face up in three rows: roots, stems and leaves. 3. Keep the trouble cards face down.
flow.say: Each of you has a hard place to live. Your job is to design a plant that can live there. Choose their root, their stem and their leaf.
flow.kid: Take a place card. That is where your plant lives. Choose one root, one stem and one leaf. Build a plant that can survive there!
flow.context: This is the first step of Build a Plant to Survive. Each player designs a plant for a hard place by choosing their root, stem and leaf.

flow.do: 1. Take turns choosing one root, one stem and one leaf card. 2. Each player draws their plant and names them.
flow.say: Why did you choose that root? What will it do for your plant in that place?
flow.kid: Pick a root, a stem and a leaf. Draw your plant. Give them a name. Say why you chose each part.

ask.q: Why is a wide, thin leaf a bad choice for the desert?
good: It would lose too much water.
The Sun would dry it out.

flow.parent: There is more than one good plant for each place. Desert: deep tap root or wide shallow roots, a fat water-storing stem, spines. Dark forest floor: wide thin leaves, or a climbing stem to reach the light. Pond: floating leaves and hollow stems. Salty mud: breathing roots and pillar roots. Windy hill: tough needles, a deep tap root.

flow.do: 1. Each player takes a trouble card and explains how their plant survives it. 2. The others vote. 3. Score one point for each part that helped.
flow.say: Here comes trouble. Can your plant survive it? Convince us!
flow.kid: Take a trouble card. Can your plant survive it? Explain how. Everyone votes.

check.q: Trouble card: no rain for six months. Which plant has the best chance?
options: A plant with wide, thin leaves and short roots
A plant with a fat water-storing stem, spines and long roots
A plant with floating leaves
check.why: A fat stem stores water for the dry months. Spines lose far less water than wide leaves, and long roots reach water deep down. That is the cactus plan. Picking wide leaves usually means thinking more leaves always help. In a drought, wide leaves lose water fastest.

flow.do: Talk about whose plants survived and why. Then look for a real plant that matches each design.
flow.say: Did any of your inventions already exist? Which real plants look like them?
flow.kid: Does a real plant look like yours? Can you name them?
flow.think: Real plants shaped their parts over many, many generations. How did they end up with parts that fit their place so well?

games.context: This is a design game. Players build an imaginary plant for a hard place, like a desert or a muddy pond, by choosing their root, stem and leaf. Then trouble comes.
