items.p: Match each part of a plant to its main job.
pairs: holds the plant in the soil and soaks up water
holds the plant up and carries water and food
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Each part has its own job. The plant needs all of them to stay alive.
items.art: A simple plant with the four parts labelled.

items.p: A potato has eyes that sprout shoots. What is a potato?
items.why: The eyes are buds, and buds grow on stems. So a potato is a stem that grows underground, called a tuber. Picking 'root' usually means deciding by where it grows. Many stems grow underground.

items.p: Everything that grows under the ground is a root.
items.why: False. Potato, ginger, turmeric and chembu grow under the ground, but they are stems. They have buds and rings. An onion's layers are leaves.

items.p: Sort these into tap root or fibrous roots.
items.a: see items
items.why: A tap root is one thick main root going down. Fibrous roots are a beard of thin roots, all about the same size.

items.p: Which one is the odd one out, and why? Mango, tomato, bhindi, carrot.
items.a: Carrot, because a carrot is a root. Mango, tomato and bhindi are fruits. Each one grew from a flower and holds seeds.
items.why: A fruit is the part that grows from a flower and carries the seeds. Cut a tomato or a bhindi open and you see the seeds. A carrot has no seeds inside, because a carrot is a root that stores food.

items.p: Why are most leaves thin and flat?
opts: To spread out and catch lots of sunlight
To be light enough to blow away
To hold the plant in the ground
items.why: A thin, flat leaf works like a solar panel. It spreads out to catch light, and light can reach every cell inside it. Picking 'to store water' mixes up ordinary leaves with thick, juicy leaves like aloe, which are a special case.

items.p: Roots help to hold soil together, so rain does not wash it away.
items.why: True. A net of roots grips the soil crumbs. In the Roots Hold the Soil test, the grass tray lost far less mud than the bare tray.
items.context: In the Roots Hold the Soil experiment, you pour water over a tray of bare soil and a tray of grass, and compare the mud that washes off.

items.p: In the Wake the Store test, which piece grew no shoot at all?
items.why: The carrot middle has stored food but no buds. New shoots grow from buds, and a carrot's buds are at its top. Picking the onion is a surprise guess. Onions usually grow first and fastest.
items.context: In the Wake the Store experiment, you stand a carrot top, a carrot middle slice, a radish top, an onion and a potato in saucers of water, and measure their new shoots.

items.p: Meenakshi, a girl in Class 3, puts a money plant cutting in a glass of water. After a week, white roots grow from the stem. What does this show?
opts: A cutting can grow the parts they are missing
The roots came from the water
The stem has turned into a root
items.why: The cutting had a stem and leaves but no roots. A plant needs roots to soak up water and hold on, so the cutting grew new ones. Picking 'never need roots' gets it backwards. The cutting grew roots because roots are needed.

items.p: Name one root and one stem that store food. Say one clue that tells you each is a root or a stem.
items.a: For example: a carrot is a root, because it has no eyes or rings along its sides. A potato is a stem, because it has eyes, which are buds.
items.why: Any correct pair with a clue for each is right. Clues for stems are buds, eyes and rings. Roots usually have none of these.

items.p: Why do you think a climbing plant has a thin stem, not a thick trunk like a tree?
items.a: A thin stem is quick and cheap to grow. The climber does not need to hold themselves up, because they lean on something else. So they reach the light faster.
items.why: A good answer links the thin shape to the job: reaching light by leaning on others.

items.p: Match each plant to the part that stores their food.
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Plants store food in different parts. The clues are eyes, rings and layers, not where the part grows.

items.p: The curly thread a pea or gourd plant uses to grab things is called a ____.
items.why: Tendrils coil round anything they touch. A pea's tendrils are changed leaf tips.

items.p: Why does a cactus have spines instead of wide leaves?
opts: Wide leaves would lose too much water in the desert
Cactuses do not need any food
items.why: Wide leaves lose lots of water into hot, dry air. Spines lose very little, and they also guard the plant from thirsty animals. The fat green stem does the leaf's food-making job. Picking 'cactuses do not need food' misses that the stem makes their food.

items.p: Two sisters, Kavya and Nila, are arguing about which part of a plant matters most.

views.says: The roots matter most. Without roots, a plant cannot drink, and they wilt in a day.
The leaves matter most. They make all the plant's food. Without leaves, the plant starves.

items.ask: Whose side are you on? Give one piece of evidence from this unit. Then say what the other sister has right.
items.a: A strong answer picks a side and gives evidence. For the roots: a cut rose with no roots lasts only a few days. For the leaves: a carrot top grows new leaves first, because the plant needs them to make food. A strong answer then admits the other side's point, because a plant needs both: the roots bring water to the leaves, and the leaves send food to the roots.
items.why: There is no single winner. Roots and leaves depend on each other. A good answer notices this, and still argues one side with real evidence.

items.p: Draw a plant with their roots, stem and leaves. Draw an arrow showing where water goes, and another showing where light comes from.
items.a: Roots in the soil, a stem, and leaves spread out. A water arrow from the roots up the stem to the leaves. A light arrow from the Sun to the leaves.
items.why: Water goes up from the roots. Light is caught by the leaves. The unit on how water travels through a plant tells this journey in full.
items.art: A blank pot with soil and a Sun in the corner.

items.p: Divya, a girl in Class 4, will trace leaves from the sunny top and the shady bottom of a mango tree. Predict which leaves will be bigger, and say why.
items.a: The shady leaves will probably be bigger and thinner. There is less light in the shade, so a bigger leaf catches more of it. The sunny leaves get plenty of light, so they can be smaller.
items.why: A strong answer makes a clear guess and links leaf size to how much light there is. In the Sun Leaf, Shade Leaf test, the shade leaves were bigger.
items.context: In the Sun Leaf, Shade Leaf experiment, you trace leaves from the sunny outside and the shady inside of one bush on squared paper, and count the squares.

items.p: Riya, a girl in Class 4, says shade leaves are bigger because the shade makes them swell up with water. How could she check her idea?
opts: Feel whether the shade leaves are thicker or thinner than the sun leaves
Count the leaves on the bush
items.why: If Riya is right, the shade leaves should be thick and puffy. In fact they are thinner than the sun leaves. So they are not swollen. They are spread out to catch more of the weak light. Counting the leaves would not test her idea at all.
items.context: Leaves on the shady inside of a bush are often bigger than leaves on their sunny outside.

items.p: Sort these underground parts into root, stem or leaf.
items.a: see items
items.why: Stems have buds and rings: potato, ginger, turmeric, chembu. Onion layers are swollen leaves. Carrot, radish and sweet potato are roots.

items.p: In the Blue-Black Test, the potato turned blue-black with iodine, but the carrot stayed brown. Which is true?
opts: The potato stores starch, and the carrot stores mostly sugar
The carrot has no food in it
The potato is a root and the carrot is a stem
items.why: Iodine turns blue-black only on starch. The carrot is full of food, but mostly sugar, which is why it tastes sweet. Picking 'no food' means reading 'no starch' as 'no food'. Picking the third option swaps the parts round.
items.context: In the Blue-Black Test, a grown-up puts drops of iodine on cut pieces of vegetables. Iodine turns blue-black where there is starch.

items.p: Match each root to its surprising job.
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Roots can hold up, breathe, climb and store, not only drink.

items.p: A lotus leaf floats on a pond. Where are its stomata, the tiny holes that let air in?
opts: On the top side, facing the air
On the bottom side, in the water
items.why: On most land leaves, stomata are mostly underneath. A floating lotus leaf has them on top, where the air is. Its shape and its holes both fit its life on water. Picking 'bottom side' means using the rule for land leaves. The lotus breaks that rule for a good reason.

items.p: A gourd tendril has grabbed a stick. The coiled part between the stem and the stick twists one way at one end and the other way at the other end.
items.why: True. Both ends are held, so it cannot twist all one way. It makes a spring with a switch point in the middle. Darwin described it, and scientists explained it in 2012.
items.context: In the Tickle a Tendril activity, you look closely at the coiled tendrils of a gourd or pea plant.

items.p: A stem that grows sideways under the ground, like ginger or turmeric, is called a ____.
items.why: Ginger and turmeric are rhizomes. Their rings are nodes, and their buds can grow new shoots.

items.p: Why does an old carrot that has flowered taste woody and not sweet?
opts: Their stored sugar was used up to grow the flower stalk and seeds
items.why: The carrot stored sugar for the next stage of their life. When they flowered, they used that food to grow a tall stalk and seeds. Picking 'insects ate it' is a reasonable guess. But the root is not damaged, it is just emptied out.
items.context: In this unit's story, Jasmeet replants ten carrots instead of selling them. They grow tall white flowers and make seed.

items.p: A jasmine (malli) flower is white and smells strongest in the evening. Who is the flower most likely calling?
opts: Moths that fly at dusk and at night
Birds that fly in the morning
items.why: A flower's job is to make seeds, and for that pollen must be carried from flower to flower. White shows up in dim light, and a strong smell carries in the dark. Night-flying moths follow both. Picking bees is a fair guess, because bees visit many flowers, but bees mostly fly in the daytime.

items.p: A rose's sharp points are thorns, just like the thorns of bougainvillea.
items.why: False. A bougainvillea thorn is a changed branch, and it grows from the point where a bud would be. A rose's sharp points grow only from the skin of the stem. You can snap one off cleanly, and there is no bud near it. Botanists call them prickles. In everyday talk, calling them thorns is fine.

items.p: Chembu leaves and lotus leaves make raindrops roll off in balls. How might that help a plant?
items.a: The rolling drops pick up dust and dirt and carry it away, so the leaf stays clean. A clean leaf catches more light. Water also does not sit on the leaf and block its tiny holes.
items.why: A good answer links the waxy shape to the leaf's job: staying clean to catch light and breathe.

items.p: Meenakshi, a girl in Class 4, says, 'Fat roots grow big so that we can eat them.' What would you tell her? Give evidence.
items.a: The root stores food for the plant's own use. A carrot left in the ground uses that food later to grow a flower stalk and seeds. We just eat the carrot before they get the chance.
items.why: A good answer says who the food is really for, and gives evidence, like a carrot that flowers.

items.p: In this unit's story, Jasmeet and her mother Harpreet grow carrots on their farm in Haryana. At harvest time, they disagree about what to do with the carrots.

views.says: Pull up and sell every fat carrot now. A carrot that is left to flower goes woody, and nobody will buy them.
Leave the ten best carrots in the ground. They will use their stored sugar to make seed, so next year we will not have to buy any.

items.ask: Which plan would you choose for the family? Use what you know about what a carrot's stored food is for. Then say what the other person has right.
items.a: A strong answer uses the science. A carrot stores sugar in their root for their own next stage. If they are left, they spend it on a flower stalk and seeds, so the root goes woody. For Jasmeet: ten carrots give a whole tin of seed, and shop seed costs a lot. For Harpreet: those ten carrots cannot be sold, and the family needs money now. A strong answer gives the other side's point too.
items.why: This is a real farmer's choice between money now and seed later. Both plans make sense. What makes an answer strong is knowing that the carrot's food is for the carrot's own flowers and seeds.
items.context: In this unit's story, Jasmeet finds an old carrot that has flowered. Their root has gone woody, and the flower has made lots of seed.

items.p: Design the roots for a plant on a windy, rocky hillside. Draw them and label how they help.
items.a: Deep roots pushing into cracks in the rock, and spreading side roots gripping the soil. Labels say they hold on against wind and reach water deep down.
items.why: Roots on windy hills must anchor the plant and find water in cracks.
items.art: An outline of a rocky hill with cracks in it.

items.p: A sweet potato is a root, but it can sprout shoots. Does that break the rule 'buds grow on stems'?
opts: It shows that rules in biology have exceptions, so botanists use several clues together
It proves a sweet potato is a stem
It proves the rule is useless
items.why: Most roots have no buds, but a few, like sweet potato, can grow shoots. Botanists look at many clues, like how it grew and what it is joined to. Picking 'the rule is useless' throws away a rule that works for most plants.

items.p: Cactuses grow in the Americas. Some euphorbias grow in Africa. Both have fat, green, spiny stems, but they are not close relatives. Explain how two plants that are not related could end up with the same shape.
items.a: Both live in hot, dry places. There, wide leaves would lose too much water, so spines and a fat stem that stores water help a plant survive. Over a very long time, the plants with those shapes survived best in both places. So the same problem gave the same answer twice.
items.why: A strong answer links the shape to the job in that place: saving and storing water. It says the shape helped each plant survive, not that one copied the other.

items.p: In the Wake the Store test, the carrot middle grew nothing. Is that a failure? What did it teach us?
items.a: No, it was our check. It had food but no buds, and it grew nothing. So it showed that new shoots need a bud, not only food.
items.why: A check that stays the same is as useful as a result that changes. It tells you what made the difference.
items.context: In the Wake the Store experiment, a carrot top and a slice from the middle of the same carrot are stood in water, with other vegetables.

items.p: Mangrove trees grow in salty mud that floods twice a day. Why do their roots poke up out of the mud?
opts: To get air, because flooded mud has almost none
items.why: Roots need air to stay alive. In waterlogged mud there is almost none, so breathing roots stick up like snorkels. Picking 'drink rainwater' is close, but these roots are mainly for air.

items.p: People have argued for over 200 years about whether petals, tendrils and spines are all leaves in disguise.

views.who: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe, a German poet and thinker, in 1790
views.says: Every part above the ground, even the parts of a flower, is the same basic leaf in a different form.

views.who: Agnes Arber, an English botanist, around 1950
views.says: A leaf is really a part of a shoot that stopped growing early. So leaves and stems are not as separate as they look.
Goethe was right about flowers. When certain genes are switched off, a flower grows only leaf-like parts. But many thorns come from stems, not leaves.

items.ask: Which idea do you find most convincing? Use one example from this unit, like a pea tendril, a cactus spine or a bougainvillea thorn. Then say what one of the others got right.
items.a: A strong answer backs one view with an example. A pea tendril grows where the last leaflets should be, and a cactus spine is a changed leaf, so Goethe was often right. But a bougainvillea thorn grows from a bud point, so it is a changed branch, which the gene scientists point out. A strong answer then gives another view its due, for example that Arber showed leaves and stems are closely linked.
items.why: Each view is partly right. Goethe's idea works for flowers and for many parts, but not for every part. What matters is using real examples as evidence.

items.p: Design a fair test to find out whether a gourd tendril curls faster when it is touched more times. What will you change? What will you keep the same?
items.a: I will change only the number of rubs: 1 rub, 5 rubs and 10 rubs, on three young tendrils of the same plant. I will keep the same plant, tendrils of the same age, the same matchstick, and check them all at 30 minutes and 2 hours.
items.why: A fair test changes one thing and keeps everything else the same.
items.context: In the Tickle a Tendril activity, you rub a young tendril 10 times with a matchstick and watch whether it curls.

items.p: The first land plants had no roots and no leaves. Which is the best evidence?
opts: Fossils of very old plants, like those found in 407-million-year-old rocks at Rhynie in Scotland
Old stories about the first plants
items.why: Rocks at Rhynie hold whole little plants turned to stone, with no true roots or leaves. Fossils are evidence you can look at. Picking 'plants today all have roots' is not true, and it tells us nothing about the past anyway.

items.p: Plants are simple, because they cannot move.
items.why: False. Plants move slowly, so we miss it. A tendril curls round a stick within hours of being touched. A bean shoot circles in loops until they find a support. Leaves turn towards the light. Plants sense touch, light and water, and they change their shape to fit their place.

items.p: Nancy Kiang, a NASA scientist, suggested that plants on a planet with a dim red star might be very dark, even black. Use what you know about leaves to explain her idea.
items.a: A leaf's job is to catch light. A dark leaf soaks up almost every colour, and lets very little bounce off. Under a dim star there is not much light, so a plant would need to catch every bit of it.
items.why: A strong answer links colour to how much light is caught. It is only an idea: no plants have been found on other planets.

items.p: A Khasi root bridge gets stronger every year. A bridge made of cut bamboo slowly rots in the rain. Why is the root bridge different?
items.a: The root bridge is made of living roots. They keep growing thicker, join together and mend damage. Cut bamboo is no longer growing, so it cannot mend itself, and it rots.
items.why: A good answer says that the roots are alive and still growing, so the bridge can grow stronger and repair itself.
items.context: In Meghalaya, Khasi and Jaintia people guide the aerial roots of rubber fig trees across streams. Over many years the roots grow thick and become bridges.

items.p: Why are spirals of leaves and scales so common in plants?
opts: They pack things tightly and stop leaves shading each other
Plants like the look of spirals
Spirals make plants grow faster upward
items.why: Each new leaf turned a little from the last means each gets its own patch of sky. Seeds and scales in spirals pack with almost no gaps. Picking 'the wind twists them' is a sensible guess, but the pattern starts in the growing tip, long before the wind can reach it.

items.p: A plant has net veins in their leaves. What roots do they probably have?
items.why: Net veins usually go with a tap root, as in mango, beans and mustard. Parallel veins usually go with fibrous roots, as in grass and maize. Picking fibrous roots means swapping the two groups. Remember: grass has parallel veins and a beard of roots.

items.p: Light is made of tiny packets called photons. Explain in your own words what a leaf does with a photon.
items.a: When a photon hits the green chlorophyll in a leaf, its energy is caught. The energy is passed along to where the leaf makes food.
items.why: Chlorophyll catches the energy of light and passes it on. The unit on photosynthesis explains how the food is made.

items.p: Why is a hollow tube a good shape for a tall stem like bamboo?
opts: It is strong against bending but uses little material
It is easier for leaves to grow on
It makes the plant heavier, so they do not blow away
items.why: Material round the outside of a tube resists bending best. So a tube is strong without being heavy. In the Paper Stem challenge, the rolled tube held the most books. Picking 'heavier' gets it backwards. Bamboo is strong because it is light for its strength.
items.context: In The Paper Stem challenge, you make stems from one sheet of paper in different shapes and test which holds the most books.

items.p: Put these in the order they first appeared on Earth, oldest first: flowers, roots, tiny stems with no leaves, wide flat leaves.
items.a: order shown
items.why: The first land plants were tiny stems. Roots came by about 400 million years ago. Wide leaves became common about 360 million years ago. Flowers came last, about 130 million years ago.

items.p: Draw a zoom into a leaf in four steps: the leaf, its cells, the green blobs inside a cell, and a chlorophyll molecule catching light.
items.a: A leaf. A wall of brick-like cells. Green blobs inside one cell. A ring-shaped molecule with a glowing photon arriving.
items.why: This shows how a leaf catches light, from what you can see down to molecules you cannot.

experiments.title: Wake the Store: can a stored food part grow with no soil?
experiments.question: Do roots and stems that store food have enough food inside to grow new shoots, with no soil at all?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. Which piece will grow the tallest shoot in 8 days: the carrot top, the carrot middle, the radish top, the onion or the potato? Will any piece grow nothing at all? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Give every piece the same: the same depth of water, the same window, and fresh water every 2 days. Change only the kind of piece. The carrot middle is our check. It is the same carrot, but with no top, so we find out where new shoots grow from.

materials.item: a carrot with its top, and a radish with its top
an onion and an old potato with eyes
5 saucers or small steel katoris, and a glass
toothpicks, to hold the potato in the glass
a ruler with millimetre marks, like the one in a school geometry box

experiments.safety: A grown-up does all the cutting. Throw the pieces away at the end. Do not eat them.

schedule.what: Guess first. A grown-up cuts the pieces. Set them in water by a window.
Measure the tallest shoot on each piece. Change the water.
Last measurements. Draw a bar chart. Say what you think, what you saw and why.

experiments.record: Fill in the table every two days. On day 8, draw one bar for each piece, as tall as its tallest shoot.

flow.do: 1. Lay out the carrot, radish, onion and potato. 2. Ask your child to guess which will grow the tallest new shoot in 8 days, and which will grow nothing.
flow.say: These vegetables are all food stores. Roots and stems pack food away for the plant's future. Do you think they still have enough food to grow, with no soil at all?
flow.kid: Look at the carrot, radish, onion and potato. They are all food stores. Can they grow without soil? Guess which grows tallest.

ask.q: Why did you pick that one?
good: It already has a little shoot.

flow.context: This is the first step of Wake the Store. You find out whether roots and stems that store food can grow new shoots with no soil.

flow.do: 1. A grown-up cuts the top 3 cm off the carrot and off the radish, keeping the leafy end. 2. Trim any old leaves to 1 cm. 3. Cut a 3 cm slice from the middle of the carrot, with no top. 4. Cut the bottom 2 cm off the onion, keeping the flat base. 5. Push 3 toothpicks into the potato and rest it on the glass, so its bottom half is in water.
flow.say: This slice from the middle of the carrot is our check. It is the same carrot, but it has no top. If only the top grows, we learn where new shoots come from.
flow.kid: A grown-up cuts the pieces. Watch the carrot middle. It is our check. Does a carrot need its top to grow?

flow.do: 1. Put the carrot top, the carrot middle and the radish top in their own saucers, cut side down. Stand the onion base on its flat bottom in the fourth saucer. The potato stays on its glass. 2. Pour water to about 1 cm deep. 3. Put all of them on the same windowsill. 4. Label each saucer.
flow.say: Same water, same window, same everything. Only the kind of piece is different. That makes it fair.
flow.kid: Put each piece, except the potato, in its own saucer. Add water, one finger-width deep. Put them all on the same windowsill.

flow.do: 1. On days 2, 4, 6 and 8, measure the tallest new shoot on each piece in millimetres. 2. Write it in the table. 3. Pour away the old water and add fresh water, to stop it smelling.
flow.say: Lay the ruler next to the shoot. Start at zero, where the shoot comes out. Read the small lines. Each one is a millimetre.
flow.kid: Every two days, measure the tallest shoot. Start the ruler at zero. Write the number. Give fresh water.
flow.wait: Measure again every 2 days, for 8 days.
flow.parent: The onion usually grows first, and fastest. The carrot and radish tops grow feathery leaves in 3 to 5 days. The potato's eyes may take a week or more, so a potato that is already sprouting a little works best. The carrot middle grows nothing, because it has no buds. If anything goes slimy, throw it away and note it in the table.

chart.title: Made-up example: how to fill in the table

flow.do: Help your child draw a bar chart of the day 8 numbers, with one bar for each piece.
flow.say: Let's turn our numbers into a picture. Each piece gets one bar, as tall as its tallest shoot.
flow.kid: Draw one bar for each piece. Make it as tall as its tallest shoot on day 8.

check.q: The carrot top grew leaves, but the carrot middle grew nothing. Why?
options: The middle had no food in it
The middle had no buds, and new shoots grow from buds at the top
The middle did not get enough water
check.why: The middle slice is full of stored food, just like the top. But new shoots grow only from buds. A carrot's buds are at its top, where a tiny squashed stem joins the leaves. Picking 'no food' usually means thinking food alone makes a plant grow. A plant needs both food and a bud to grow from.

chart.title: Made-up example results: tallest new shoot after 8 days
chart.note: These numbers are made up, to show what a finished chart can look like. Your numbers will be different.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: Now tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see that shows it? And why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Now write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: This is called claim, evidence and reasoning. Any honest answer with all three parts is good. A good answer sounds like this. What I think: food stores can grow new shoots without soil, but only from a bud. What I saw: the onion grew 60 mm and the carrot top 40 mm. The carrot middle grew nothing. Why: the stored food feeds the new shoot, and the shoot grows from the bud at the top.

experiments.context: This is the Wake the Store experiment. You stand pieces of carrot, radish, onion and potato in saucers of water for 8 days and measure the new shoots they grow.

experiments.title: The Blue-Black Test: where does a plant keep their starch?
experiments.question: Which roots and stems store their food as starch, and which store it as sugar?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Iodine turns blue-black where there is starch. Which pieces will turn blue-black: potato, carrot, sweet potato, ginger, onion or raw banana? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Cut every piece fresh, the same size. Put the same number of drops, three, on each. Wait the same time, one minute, before you look.

materials.item: povidone-iodine solution from a chemist, mixed 1 spoon with 4 spoons of water in a small cup
a dropper, or a cotton bud
small pieces of potato, carrot, sweet potato, ginger, onion and raw banana
an old plate or tray, and newspaper

experiments.safety: A grown-up cuts the pieces and handles the iodine. Iodine stains clothes and skin, so cover the table with newspaper. Never eat any piece after testing. Throw them all away and wash hands.

schedule.what: Guess, test six pieces with iodine, and fill in the table.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Colour a small square next to each piece to match the colour you saw.

flow.do: 1. Cover the table with newspaper. 2. A grown-up cuts a fresh, flat piece of each vegetable, about the size of a coin. 3. Lay them on an old plate and label each one.
flow.say: Plants store food in two main ways. Sugar tastes sweet. Starch does not taste sweet, but it fills you up, like rice and ragi. Iodine is a test. It turns blue-black where there is starch.
flow.kid: A grown-up cuts six pieces. Starch is food that is not sweet, like in rice. Iodine turns blue-black on starch. Guess which pieces will change.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Blue-Black Test. You use iodine from the chemist to find out which roots and stems store starch.

flow.do: Ask your child to write their guess for each piece in the table: lots of starch, some or none.
flow.say: Think about how each one tastes. Which ones are sweet? Which are not sweet but filling?
flow.kid: Write your guess for each piece. Sweet ones might have sugar. Filling ones might have starch.

ask.q: Why do you think the carrot will or will not turn black?
good: It tastes sweet, so maybe it stores sugar.
It is a food store, so maybe it has starch.

flow.do: 1. A grown-up puts 3 drops of the iodine mix on each piece. 2. Wait one minute. 3. Look at each piece in daylight. 4. Write down the colour.
flow.say: Watch the potato. And now watch the carrot. Are they the same?
flow.kid: A grown-up drops iodine on each piece. Wait one minute. What colour is each one now?
flow.parent: Expect the potato, sweet potato and raw banana to turn dark blue-black within seconds. Ginger turns dark too. The carrot and onion stay brownish-orange, the colour of the iodine. They store their food mostly as sugar, which is why they taste sweet.

check.q: The potato turned blue-black. The carrot stayed brown. What does this tell us?
options: The carrot has no stored food
The potato stores starch, and the carrot stores its food in another way, mostly as sugar
The iodine did not work on the carrot
check.why: Both are food stores. The potato packs its food as starch, so iodine turns it blue-black. The carrot packs most of its food as sugar, which is why it tastes sweet. Iodine does not change colour on sugar. Picking 'no stored food' means taking 'no starch' to mean 'no food'. Taste a raw carrot and you know it is full of food.

flow.do: Sort the pieces into two groups: blue-black and not blue-black. Then say for each piece whether it is a root, a stem or a leaf.
flow.say: Look at the groups. Did all the roots do one thing and all the stems another? Or is it mixed?
flow.kid: Sort the pieces. Blue-black, or not? Now say which are roots, stems or leaves. Is there a pattern?
flow.think: The potato is a stem and the sweet potato is a root, but both are full of starch. So does the kind of food tell you which part it is?

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: Now tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see that shows it? And why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Now write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: This is called claim, evidence and reasoning. Any honest answer with all three parts is good. A good answer sounds like this. What I think: roots and stems store food in different ways. What I saw: the potato, sweet potato and ginger turned blue-black, but the carrot and onion stayed brown. Why: some plants store their food as starch and some store it as sugar.

experiments.context: In this experiment, you put drops of iodine on cut pieces of vegetables. Iodine turns blue-black where there is starch, a kind of stored food. It shows how roots and stems keep their food.

setup.caption: 1. A grown-up cuts six small pieces and labels them.

setup.art: A grown-up's hand holding a dropper of brown iodine over a potato slice, a child watching from a safe distance.
setup.caption: 2. A grown-up puts 3 drops of iodine on each piece.

experiments.title: Sun Leaf, Shade Leaf
experiments.question: Are leaves that grow in the shade a different size from leaves that grow in the sun, on the same plant?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Will the leaves from the shady inside of a bush be bigger, smaller or the same size as the leaves from their sunny outside? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Take all the leaves from the same plant. Take 5 from the sunny outside and 5 from the shady inside. Pick fully grown leaves, not baby ones. Measure every leaf the same way, by counting squares.

materials.item: a bush or a low tree with simple leaves, like hibiscus, guava or mango, near your building or in a park. This test needs a plant with a sunny outside and a shady inside, so do it when you can reach one
squared paper with 1 cm squares, or plain paper on which you draw 1 cm squares with a ruler
a pencil

experiments.safety: Pick only 10 leaves, and ask the owner of the plant first. Wash hands after handling leaves.

schedule.what: Pick 5 sun leaves and 5 shade leaves. Trace them and count the squares. Draw a bar chart.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Put each group's numbers in order and circle the middle one. Draw two bars, one for the middle sun leaf and one for the middle shade leaf.

flow.do: 1. Find a big bush or low tree. 2. Pick 5 fully grown leaves from the sunny outside. 3. Pick 5 from deep inside, where it is shady. 4. Keep the two groups apart.
flow.say: These leaves all come from the same plant. The only difference is where they grew: in the sun or in the shade. Guess first. Which group will be bigger?
flow.kid: Pick 5 big leaves from the sunny outside of a bush. Pick 5 from the shady inside. Keep them in two piles. Which pile looks bigger?
flow.context: This is the first step of Sun Leaf, Shade Leaf. You compare leaves from the sunny outside and the shady inside of one plant.

flow.do: 1. Lay a leaf flat on the squared paper. 2. Draw round it with a pencil. 3. Count the squares inside the line. Count a square if half or more of it is inside. 4. Write the number inside the drawing. 5. Do this for all 10 leaves.
flow.say: Counting squares tells us how much space a leaf covers. Scientists call that its area. A half square or more counts as one. Less than half, we leave out.
flow.kid: Lay a leaf on the squared paper. Draw round it. Count the squares inside. Half a square or more counts as one.
flow.parent: Counting squares measures area, how much flat space a leaf covers. Children often miscount the edges. That is fine, as long as they use the same rule every time.

flow.do: Hold one sun leaf and one shade leaf up to a window, one after the other.
flow.say: Which leaf lets more light through? Which feels thinner between your fingers?
flow.kid: Hold a sun leaf up to the window. Now a shade leaf. Which lets more light through? Which feels thinner?

ask.q: Why might a shade leaf be bigger and thinner?
good: To catch more of the weak light.
There is not much light in the shade, so it spreads out wide.

flow.do: 1. Put the 5 sun numbers in order and circle the middle one. 2. Do the same for the shade numbers. 3. Draw a bar for each middle number.
flow.say: The middle number is fairer than picking one leaf. One leaf could be unusual.
flow.kid: Put the 5 sun numbers in order. Circle the middle one. Do the same for shade. Draw two bars.

check.q: On one hibiscus bush, the middle sun leaf covered 18 squares and the middle shade leaf covered 27. What does this suggest?
options: Shade leaves grow bigger, to catch more of the weak light
Sun leaves are bigger, because they get more food
Leaves are always the same size
check.why: In the shade there is less light, so a plant grows bigger, thinner leaves to catch as much as they can. In full sun there is plenty of light, so smaller, thicker leaves are enough, and they lose less water. Picking 'sun leaves are bigger' is a sensible guess, because the sun gives more energy. But a leaf's size is about how much light it needs to catch.

flow.say: Now tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see that shows it? And why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Now write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: This is called claim, evidence and reasoning. Any honest answer with all three parts is good. A good answer sounds like this. What I think: leaves in the shade grow bigger. What I saw: the middle shade leaf covered 27 squares and the middle sun leaf covered only 18. The shade leaf was thinner too. Why: there is less light in the shade, so a bigger leaf catches more of it.

experiments.title: Roots Hold the Soil
experiments.question: Do roots really hold soil together when water rushes over it?
experiments.predict: Guess first. When we pour water over a slope of bare soil and a slope of soil with roots, which will lose more soil? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Use two trays of the same size and the same soil, tilted on the same books. Pour the same amount of water, from the same height, at the same speed. Change only one thing: one tray has grass with roots, the other is bare.
results_table: How muddy was the water? (clear, a bit muddy, very muddy)
Height of mud at the bottom of the glass after 10 minutes (mm)

materials.item: two shallow plastic trays or ice-cream boxes, each with a small notch cut in one end

a clump of grass dug up with their soil and roots. In a flat, grow your own instead: 10 days before, scatter a thick layer of wheat, methi or mustard seeds on soil in one tray and water a little every day. The seedlings make a mat of roots. You also need the same amount of bare soil, from a pot or a bag of potting soil
two clear glasses, two mugs of water and a few books
a ruler, and a hand lens if you have one

experiments.safety: Do this outside or on the balcony. A grown-up digs the grass and cuts the notches. Wash hands after handling soil.

schedule.what: Look at the roots, set up two tilted trays, pour the water and compare the mud.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Draw both glasses, showing how much mud settled at the bottom.

flow.do: 1. A grown-up digs up a small clump of grass with their soil, or lifts the mat of seedlings you grew. 2. Gently shake soil off one corner. 3. Look at the roots, with a hand lens if you have one. 4. If you have a moong sprout, look at their root too, against black paper.
flow.say: Look how many thin roots there are. They spread out like a net. And look at the tiny white fuzz on the sprout. Those are root hairs.
flow.kid: Look at the grass roots with a hand lens. How many can you count? Look at a moong sprout's root too. See the fuzz?

ask.q: Why might a net of thin roots be better than one thick root, for holding soil?
good: The thin roots go everywhere and hold the crumbs together.

flow.context: This is the first step of Roots Hold the Soil. You look closely at grass roots before testing whether they stop soil being washed away.
flow.parent: If you have no grass nearby, sow wheat, methi or mustard seeds thickly in the tray about 10 days before. They sprout in 2 to 3 days in warm weather and make a thick mat of roots.

flow.do: 1. Pack the grass clump into one tray. 2. Pack the same amount of bare soil into the other. 3. Rest both trays on the same pile of books, with the notches at the low end. 4. Put a glass under each notch.
flow.say: Both trays are the same, except one has roots. That is the one thing we change.
flow.kid: Put the grass in one tray and bare soil in the other. Tilt both on the same books. Put a glass under each notch.

flow.do: 1. Pour one mug of water slowly over the top end of the bare tray. 2. Pour another mug the same way over the grass tray. 3. Watch the water run into the glasses.
flow.say: Pour slowly and from the same height each time. That is like a rain shower falling on a hillside.
flow.kid: Pour one mug of water slowly onto the top of each tray. Watch what runs into the glasses.

flow.do: 1. Wait 10 minutes for the mud to settle. 2. Measure the height of the mud layer at the bottom of each glass, in millimetres. 3. Write both numbers in the table.
flow.say: Which glass is muddier? Where did that mud come from?
flow.kid: Wait 10 minutes. Measure the mud at the bottom of each glass. Which has more?

check.q: The glass under the bare tray had 12 mm of mud. The glass under the grass tray had 2 mm. Why?
options: The grass roots held the soil together
The grass drank all the water
The bare soil was heavier
check.why: Grass has fibrous roots, a net of thin roots that grips soil crumbs. So the water ran off, but the soil mostly stayed. Bare soil had nothing to hold it, so the water carried it away. Picking 'drank all the water' is a common guess. But the grass glass still filled with water. It was just clearer.

chart.y: Mud at the bottom of the glass (mm)

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: Now tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see that shows it? And why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Now write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: This is called claim, evidence and reasoning. Any honest answer with all three parts is good. A good answer sounds like this. What I think: roots hold soil together. What I saw: the bare tray lost 12 mm of mud and the grass tray only 2 mm. Why: the grass roots make a net that grips the soil, so the water cannot carry it away.

activities.title: Vegetable Detectives: root or stem?

materials.item: a carrot, a radish, a potato, a sweet potato, a piece of ginger, an onion, a spring onion and a small piece of sugarcane if you can find it
a hand lens, if you have one
a knife, used only by a grown-up

activities.safety: A grown-up does all the cutting.

schedule.what: Find the clues on each vegetable, cut a carrot and an onion, and sort them into roots, stems and leaves.

activities.record: Draw each vegetable. Draw an arrow to the clue that told you what it is.

flow.do: Lay the vegetables in a row. Tell your child the three detective clues.
flow.say: Here are the clues. Stems have nodes, which look like rings or bumps. Stems have buds, which look like eyes. Roots usually have neither, but they often have tiny hair-like side roots.
flow.kid: You are a plant detective. Clue one: stems have rings. Clue two: stems have buds, like eyes. Roots usually have neither.
flow.context: This is the first step of Vegetable Detectives. You use clues to find out whether kitchen vegetables are roots, stems or leaves.

flow.do: 1. Look at each vegetable closely, with a hand lens if you have one. 2. Look for eyes, rings and tiny side roots. 3. On the potato, join its eyes with a finger. Do they go round in a spiral?
flow.say: Look closely. Does it have eyes? Rings? Tiny root hairs? Write down what you find.
flow.kid: Look at each one with the hand lens. Find eyes, rings or tiny hairs. Join the potato's eyes with your finger. Is it a spiral?

good: Ginger has rings all along it.

flow.parent: Potato: eyes in a spiral, so a stem. Ginger: rings and buds, so a stem. Sugarcane: rings and buds at the nodes, so a stem. Carrot and radish: no eyes along the sides, faint lines of tiny side roots, so roots. Sweet potato: a root, though it can sprout from odd places, so it is a tricky one. Onion: layers on a flat base, so leaves on a tiny stem.

flow.do: 1. A grown-up cuts a carrot across the middle and an onion from top to bottom. 2. Look at the carrot's ring and core. 3. Look at the onion's flat base and layers. 4. Peel a spring onion to see the green leaves join the white layers.
flow.say: The carrot has a ring inside. The pale core in the middle is the bundle of tubes that carries water. The onion's layers start at that flat base. That base is its stem.
flow.kid: Look inside the carrot. See the ring and the middle? Now look at the onion. The flat bottom is its stem. The layers are leaves!

check.q: An onion's juicy layers grow from a flat base, and in a spring onion they turn into green leaves. So what are the layers?
options: Roots
Leaves that store food
Seeds
check.why: Each layer of an onion is the swollen bottom of a leaf. In a spring onion you can follow the white layer up into the green leaf. The flat base is a tiny stem, and the real roots hang below it. Picking 'roots' usually means deciding by where it grows. Underground does not always mean root.

flow.do: Sort the vegetables onto three papers: ROOT, STEM and LEAF.
flow.say: Put each one where it belongs. Tell me the clue you used.
flow.kid: Sort them onto three papers: ROOT, STEM, LEAF. Say your clue for each one.
flow.think: Why would a plant keep their food under the ground, instead of up in the air?

activities.context: This is a kitchen detective activity. You look for clues like eyes, rings and layers to decide whether vegetables are roots, stems or leaves.

activities.title: Leaf Detective Album

materials.item: a cloth bag or paper pouch for collecting
a notebook, tape and a pencil
a hand lens, if you have one

activities.safety: Go outdoors only with a grown-up. Pick fallen leaves where you can. Do not touch plants with milky sap or itchy hairs, and wash hands afterwards.

schedule.what: Collect 10 different leaves on a walk, and make an album page for each one.

activities.record: Make one album page for each leaf: the leaf taped down, its shape, its veins, where it grew, and a pet name.

flow.do: 1. Walk round the building, street or park with a cloth bag. 2. Collect 10 leaves that are as different as possible. 3. For each one, note where it grew: in sun or shade, near water or on dry ground.
flow.say: Let's find the most different leaves we can. Big and small, round and pointy, shiny and hairy. Remember where each one grew.
flow.kid: Go on a leaf hunt with a grown-up. Find 10 leaves that are all different. Remember where each one grew. Sun or shade?
flow.context: This is the first step of the Leaf Detective Album. You collect different leaves on a walk and look at how their shapes suit where they grew.

flow.do: 1. Tape each leaf onto a page. 2. Fold a spare leaf in half along its middle vein. Are the two halves the same? 3. Write three describing words for each leaf, like pointy, waxy, hairy or heart-shaped. 4. Draw its veins: a net or parallel lines.
flow.say: Describe each leaf like a detective. Fold one in half. Is it the same on both sides? Look at the veins. Do they make a net, or run side by side?
flow.kid: Tape each leaf on a page. Fold one in half. Are the halves the same? Write three words for each leaf. Draw its veins.

ask.q: Which leaf do you think grew in the most shade? Why?
good: The biggest, thinnest one, because it needs to catch more light.

flow.parent: Net veins usually go with tap roots, as in mango, hibiscus and beans. Parallel veins usually go with fibrous roots, as in grass, maize and banana. These are the two big groups of flowering plants.

flow.do: 1. Give each leaf a pet name and a short profile: where it lives and what its shape is good for. 2. Draw a little map of where you found each leaf.
flow.say: If this leaf had a profile, what would it say? 'I live in the shade, so I am big and thin.'
flow.kid: Give each leaf a pet name. Write one line about it. 'I am Waxy Wanda. I live in the sun.' Then draw a map.

check.q: A leaf is shiny and waxy on top. Where might it have grown?
options: In hot sun, where a waxy skin keeps water in
In a dark cupboard
Under the ground
check.why: A waxy skin works like a raincoat. It stops water escaping from the leaf in hot sun and wind. On lotus and chembu leaves, wax also makes rain roll off. Picking 'dark cupboard' cannot be right, because leaves need light and grow where there is light.

activities.context: This is a leaf hunt and album. You collect ten different leaves, describe them, give them pet names and think about how each shape suits where it grew.

activities.title: Tickle a Tendril

materials.item: a climbing plant with young, straight tendrils: bottle gourd, ridge gourd, cucumber, bitter gourd or pea
a matchstick or a thin twig
a piece of thread and a pencil
a hand lens, if you have one

activities.safety: Be gentle with the plant. Ask before touching a plant that belongs to someone else.

schedule.what: Tickle a tendril, check it after 30 minutes and 2 hours, and look for a coiled tendril's switch point.

activities.record: Draw the tendril before, after 30 minutes and after 2 hours. Draw a coiled tendril and mark its switch point.

flow.do: 1. Find a young tendril that is still fairly straight. 2. Rub one side of its tip gently with a matchstick, 10 times. 3. Tie a loose loop of thread near it, so it has something to grab. 4. Draw it now.
flow.say: Charles Darwin did exactly this, about 160 years ago. He tickled tendrils and timed them. Let's see if our plant feels the touch.
flow.kid: Find a straight young tendril. Rub its tip gently with a matchstick, 10 times. Draw it now. Will it move?
flow.context: This is the first step of Tickle a Tendril. A tendril is the curly thread a climbing plant uses to grab things. You test whether it feels a touch.

flow.do: After 30 minutes, look again and draw it. Then look again after 2 hours.
flow.say: Has it curled at all? Which way did it bend: towards the side we rubbed, or away?
flow.kid: Look again after 30 minutes. Has it curled? Draw it. Look again after 2 hours.
flow.wait: Look again after 30 minutes, then after 2 hours.
flow.parent: Many tendrils start to bend within an hour, curving towards the rubbed side. If nothing happens, the tendril may be too old. Try a younger one. A tendril that does not move is still a result, so write it down.

flow.do: 1. Find a tendril that has already coiled round something, so both ends are fixed. 2. Follow its coil with your finger from the plant to the support. 3. Find the place where the twist changes direction.
flow.say: Follow the coil. It twists one way, and then, in the middle, it switches and twists the other way. Darwin saw this switch. Scientists only worked out exactly why in 2012.
flow.kid: Find a tendril that has coiled round something. Follow its coil with your finger. Can you find where the twist changes direction?

check.q: A coiled tendril twists one way, then switches and twists the other way. Why?
options: Both its ends are held, so it cannot twist all one way
It got confused
The wind blew it backwards
check.why: Once a tendril has grabbed a support, one end is fixed to the plant and the other to the support. A thread held at both ends cannot twist all one way, so it makes a spring that switches direction in the middle. The spring pulls the plant closer and lets it stretch in the wind. Picking 'the wind' is a fair guess, but tendrils indoors switch too.

flow.do: Pull gently on a coiled tendril and let it go.
flow.say: Feel how it stretches and springs back, like a spring. Why might that help the plant in a storm?
flow.kid: Pull very gently on a coiled tendril. Let go. Does it spring back? How would that help in a storm?
flow.think: The tendril has no eyes and no brain. How do you think it knows it has touched something?

activities.context: In this activity you gently tickle the tendril of a gourd or pea plant and watch whether it curls. You also look for a strange switch in the twist of a coiled tendril.

activities.title: Look Down on a Plant: jigsaws and spirals

materials.item: a pot plant to look down on, like tulsi, a succulent or a rose
a pineapple, a pine cone or a cauliflower, whichever you can find
two felt pens of different colours

activities.safety: Pineapple leaves are sharp at the tips. Hold the pineapple by its body.

schedule.what: Look down on a plant, follow the leaf spiral up a stem, and count the spirals on a pineapple or pine cone.

activities.record: Draw the plant from above. Write how many spirals you counted each way.

flow.do: 1. Stand over a pot plant and look straight down. 2. Count how many leaves are hidden under others, and how many can see the sky.
flow.say: Look down like the Sun does. Do the leaves hide each other, or do they fit together like a jigsaw?
flow.kid: Look straight down on a plant, like the Sun. Do the leaves hide each other? Or fit like a jigsaw?
flow.context: This is the first step of Look Down on a Plant. You look at how leaves are arranged so they do not block each other's light.

flow.do: 1. Pick a long stem. 2. Start at the bottom leaf. 3. Go up, leaf by leaf, turning the stem in your fingers. 4. Count the leaves until you reach one sitting right above the first.
flow.say: Each new leaf is turned round a little from the one below. That way each one gets its own patch of sky.
flow.kid: Start at the bottom leaf. Go up one leaf at a time. Count until a leaf sits right above the first one.
flow.parent: In many plants, each new leaf turns a little more than a third of a circle from the last. Tulsi is different: their leaves come in pairs, each pair at right angles to the pair below. Both patterns stop leaves shading each other.

flow.do: 1. On a pineapple or a pine cone, mark one spiral going to the right with one colour. 2. Count how many spirals go that way. 3. Mark and count the spirals going the other way with the second colour.
flow.say: Count the spirals one way, then the other. Write both numbers down. Scientists find the same few numbers again and again.
flow.kid: Find the spirals on a pineapple. Count the ones going right. Now count the ones going left. Write both numbers.

check.q: You count 8 spirals one way and 13 the other way on a pineapple. These numbers are in a famous pattern: 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13. What comes next?
check.why: In this pattern, each number is the two before it added together. 1 + 1 = 2, 2 + 3 = 5, 5 + 8 = 13. So the next is 8 + 13 = 21. It is called the Fibonacci pattern. Picking 14 means adding one each time. Picking 18 means adding five. Check by adding the two numbers before.

flow.do: Talk about why plants might grow in spirals.
flow.say: Things that grow in spirals like this pack tightly, with almost no gaps. Leaves in a spiral shade each other least. The great mathematician Alan Turing was studying these spirals in the last years of his life.
flow.kid: Spirals pack things tightly with few gaps. Leaves in a spiral shade each other less. A great mathematician, Alan Turing, studied these spirals.
flow.think: Many sunflowers have Fibonacci spirals, but not all. Why might a plant break the pattern?

activities.context: In this activity you look down on plants from above and find the jigsaw and spiral patterns that help leaves catch light.

activities.title: Be the Plant: roots, climbers and sun-catchers

materials.item: some open space, a broom or a stick, and a torch to be the Sun
building blocks or kitchen boxes, if you have them

activities.safety: Move slowly. Hold the broom low, and keep it away from faces.

schedule.what: Act out roots, climbing stems and sun-catching leaves. Then build a plant from blocks.

activities.record: Draw the plant shape you liked being best, and label its jobs.

flow.do: 1. Your child stands in tree pose, one foot pressed to the other leg, arms up like branches. 2. Gently push their shoulder. 3. Then let them stand on both feet, spread wide like roots, and push again.
flow.say: You are a tree. Your feet are roots. With one foot down, a push wobbles you. Spread your roots wide. Now can I push you over?
flow.kid: Stand like a tree on one foot. A grown-up gives a gentle push. Now spread both feet wide like roots. Is it harder to push you?
flow.context: This is the first step of Be the Plant. You act out how roots, stems and leaves are shaped for their jobs.

flow.do: 1. Stand the broom upright, held by a grown-up. 2. Your child is a climber. They twine one arm round it, or curl their fingers round it like a tendril. 3. The grown-up shines the torch from high up. The child climbs towards it.
flow.say: You are a bean. You have a thin stem, so you cannot stand tall alone. Wind round the broom and climb to the Sun!
flow.kid: Be a bean plant. Wind your arm round the broom like a spiral. Climb towards the torch Sun!

flow.do: 1. The grown-up calls out a place: desert, dark forest, pond, windy hill. 2. Your child changes shape to fit. 3. Then build a plant from blocks or boxes and name each part's job.
flow.say: Desert! Make yourself small and spiky, and hold your water in. Dark forest! Spread your arms wide to catch the little light. Pond! Lie flat and float.
flow.kid: Listen for the place. Desert? Curl up small and spiky. Dark forest? Spread your arms wide. Pond? Float flat like a lotus leaf.

check.q: In the dark forest you spread your arms wide. Why do plants on a dark forest floor often have big, wide leaves?
options: To catch as much of the weak light as they can
To keep the rain off
Because they are lazy
check.why: Under tall trees, very little light reaches the ground. A big, wide, thin leaf catches as much of it as possible. Picking 'to keep the rain off' is a fair guess, because big leaves do shelter things. But their main job is to catch light.

activities.context: This is a movement activity. You use your body to act out how a root grips, how a climbing stem winds up a support and how leaves reach for light.

setup.art: A child in tree pose on one foot with arms up, then standing with feet spread wide like roots.
setup.caption: 1. Stand like a tree. Spread your feet wide like roots.

projects.title: The Climbing Bean Diary

materials.item: 6 seeds of a climbing bean: sem or a pole bean from a nursery or seed shop. Dry lobia from the kitchen may also work, but some kinds stay bushy and do not climb
2 pots or big cups of soil, with a hole in the bottom
a thin bamboo stick or a straight twig, about as tall as your child
a square of card and a felt pen, for tracing the tip
a ruler

projects.safety: Wash hands after handling soil. Raw beans are not safe to eat, so plant them, do not taste them.

schedule.what: Soak the seeds overnight. Plant 3 in each pot. Push a stick into one pot only.
Look for shoots. Water if the soil is dry. Measure the tallest shoot.
Trace the circling tip on a card above the plant for one afternoon.
Which way is the stem winding? What is the plant with no stick doing?
Measure, draw, and give the stickless plant a support. Write your diary report.

projects.record: Keep a diary page for each visit: the date, the height of the tallest stem, a drawing, and one thing you noticed.

flow.do: 1. Soak 6 bean seeds in water overnight. 2. Plant 3 in each pot, a finger-joint deep. 3. Push the stick into one pot only, next to the seeds. 4. Water both pots and put them in a sunny spot.
flow.say: One pot gets a stick to climb. The other gets nothing. We will see what a climber does when they have something to hold, and when they do not.
flow.kid: Plant 3 soaked beans in each pot. Push a stick into one pot only. Water both. Put them in the sun.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Climbing Bean Diary. Over three weeks you grow climbing beans, one pot with a stick and one without, and watch how a climber finds their support.

flow.do: 1. Look for shoots. 2. Measure the tallest one from the soil to the tip. 3. Write it in the diary.
flow.say: The shoot came up bent, like a hook. That hook protects its tip as it pushes through the soil.
flow.kid: Are the shoots up? Measure the tallest one. Write it in your diary. Water if the soil feels dry.

flow.do: 1. When a stem is long and waving, tape the card flat above the plant, without touching them. 2. Every 30 minutes, put a dot on the card right above the stem's tip. 3. Number the dots. 4. Join them at the end of the afternoon.
flow.say: Charles Darwin traced shoot tips just like this. A climbing shoot does not grow straight up. Its tip sweeps round in slow circles, feeling for something to hold.
flow.kid: Tape a card above the plant. Every 30 minutes, put a dot above the tip. Join the dots at the end. Did the tip go round in circles?
flow.wait: Do this when the stems are long, at about day 12.
flow.parent: The tip sweeps round slowly. In many beans, one circle takes an hour or two. Your dots may make a loop or a wobbly circle. Even a half circle is a good result.

flow.do: 1. Look at the plant with the stick. Look down from above. Are they winding the same way as a clock's hands, or the other way? 2. Look at the pot without a stick.
flow.say: Which way is that plant winding? Most twining plants in the world wind the same way. And look at the plants with no stick. What are they doing?
flow.kid: Look down from above. Do they wind like a clock's hands, or the other way? What are the stickless beans doing?

check.q: The beans with no stick have long, floppy stems lying over the edge of the pot. Why?
options: They are thin stems built for climbing, and have nothing to hold on to
They need more water
They are a different kind of bean
check.why: A climber saves food by growing a thin stem instead of a strong trunk. They are built to lean on something. With nothing to hold, they flop over and keep searching. Picking 'more water' is a fair guess, because floppy plants are often thirsty. But these stems are firm and green. They are just not built to stand alone.

flow.do: 1. Measure both pots. 2. Give the stickless pot a stick, and watch them grab hold over the next few days. 3. Your child writes a short diary report. It says what happened, what surprised them, and why a climber has their shape.
flow.say: Let's write it up like a botanist. What did the climbing shoot do? What did the floppy one do? Why is a thin, twining stem a good plan?
flow.kid: Measure both pots. Give the floppy beans a stick. Write your report. What surprised you most?
flow.think: The bean with no stick kept growing long and thin. What do you think they were spending their food on?

projects.context: In this three-week project, you grow climbing beans in two pots, one with a stick and one without. You trace the circling tip and watch which way the stem winds.

challenges.title: Design a Plant for a Hard Place
challenges.problem: Choose a hard place to live: a hot desert, a dark forest floor, a muddy pond, salty mud by the sea, or a windy rocky hillside. Design a plant that could live there. Draw their root, their stem and their leaves, and say what each part's shape is for.
constraints: Your plant must get water, light and air in that place.
They must survive one trouble: a drought, a goat, a flood or a storm.
Every part needs a reason. 'It looks nice' does not count.
materials: clay, paper or kitchen scraps to build a model, if you like
general: Desert: a deep tap root, a fat stem that stores water, and spines instead of wide leaves, like a cactus.
Dark forest floor: big, thin leaves to catch weak light, or a climbing stem that reaches up to the light.
Pond: round floating leaves with a waxy top, and hollow stems full of air, like a lotus.
Salty mud: breathing roots that poke up into the air, and pillar roots for support, like a mangrove.
creative: A plant whose leaves fold up like a fan at midday and open in the evening.
A plant that stores water in a balloon-like root, like some real desert plants do.
A climber that copies the Khasi root bridges, growing roots across a gap to make a path for other plants.
challenges.your_turn: Now design your own plant for a place nobody has chosen yet: a city roof, a crack in a road, or another planet with a red star. Draw it, label each part and explain why it has that shape.

flow.do: Your child picks one hard place and lists its problems.
flow.say: First, be a scientist about the place. What is hard about living there? Not enough water? Not enough light? Too much water?
flow.kid: Pick a hard place. Write its problems. Too dry? Too dark? Too wet? Too windy?
flow.context: This is the first step of the Design a Plant challenge. You choose a hard place and work out what makes living there difficult.

flow.do: 1. Your child draws a root, a stem and leaves to beat each problem. 2. They label each part with its job.
flow.say: For each problem, give your plant a part that solves it. Label it. Say why that shape helps.
flow.kid: Draw your plant. Give them a part for each problem. Label each part with its job.

check.q: A plant lives in salty mud that floods twice a day, with almost no air in the soil. Which root would help most?
options: Roots that poke up out of the mud into the air
One very deep tap root
A fat storage root
check.why: In flooded mud, the soil has almost no air, and roots need air to stay alive. Breathing roots poke up above the mud and let air in, like snorkels. Mangroves in the Sundarbans do this. Picking a deep tap root is good thinking for a desert, but here a deeper root only goes further from the air.

flow.do: Read the usual solutions and the creative ideas together. Compare them with your child's design.
flow.say: Here is how real plants solve this. Did you think of the same answers? Did you think of something nature has not tried?
flow.kid: Read how real plants solve it. Did you have the same idea? Did you invent something new?

flow.do: Your child presents the plant to the family. The family plays 'trouble' and asks how they survive.
flow.say: Tell us about your plant. We will bring trouble. A drought! A goat! How does your plant survive?
flow.kid: Show your plant to the family. They will bring trouble. Explain how your plant survives.
flow.think: Real plants did not design themselves. How did they end up so well matched to their places?

challenges.context: This is a design challenge. You invent a plant for a hard place, like a desert or salty mud, and give every part a shape that solves a problem there.

challenges.title: The Paper Stem
challenges.problem: Using only one sheet of paper and a little tape, make a stem that stands up by itself and holds up the most books. A stem's job is to hold the plant up. What shape works best?
constraints: Use one A4 sheet of paper for each stem.
The stem must be at least 15 cm tall.
Put the books on a piece of card on top, one at a time, gently.
materials: A4 paper, sticky tape and a ruler
a piece of card, about the size of a book
some light books or notebooks, all about the same weight
general: A rolled tube, like a bamboo or grass stem, usually holds the most.
A folded zigzag, like the ridges on some stems, stands up but bends easily.
A flat sheet cannot stand at all.
creative: Roll three thin tubes and tape them together, like the bundles inside a stem.
Add paper rings round the tube, like the nodes on bamboo and sugarcane.
Make a tube with a paper 'pith' stuffed loosely inside, and test whether it helps.
challenges.your_turn: Now invent your own stem shape. Test it against the tube. Can you beat it with the same sheet of paper?

flow.do: Try to stand a flat sheet of paper on its edge. Then ask your child to guess which shape will hold the most books. Will it be a tube, a zigzag or a square column?
flow.say: A flat sheet cannot even hold itself up. But the same paper, in the right shape, might hold up books. Which shape do you think will win?
flow.kid: Try to stand a flat sheet up. It flops! Guess: which shape holds the most books? A tube, a zigzag or a square?
flow.context: This is the first step of The Paper Stem. You test which shape of paper stem holds up the most books, just as a real stem holds up a plant.

flow.do: 1. Make three stems, each from one sheet: a rolled tube, a folded zigzag and a square column. Tape each one. 2. Stand one up. 3. Put the card on top and add books one at a time, until it crumples. 4. Write down how many books it held. 5. Test the others the same way.
flow.say: Add the books gently, one at a time. The same card and the same books every time, so the test is fair.
flow.kid: Make a tube, a zigzag and a square from three sheets. Stand one up. Add books one at a time. Count until it crumples.
flow.parent: A rolled tube often holds several books. The zigzag usually folds quickly. If it gets wobbly, steady the books from the side, but do not press down.

flow.do: Compare the results. Then look at a piece of bamboo, a grass stem or a stick of sugarcane together.
flow.say: Bamboo and grass stems are tubes. Many stems are strong round the outside and lighter in the middle. Why do you think plants use this shape?
flow.kid: Which shape held the most? Now look at a grass stem or bamboo. Is it a tube too?

check.q: Why are bamboo and many grass stems shaped like tubes?
options: A tube is very strong for its weight, so the plant can grow tall cheaply
Tubes are easier for insects to live in
Tubes catch more sunlight
check.why: A tube spreads its material round the outside, where it resists bending best. So it is strong without using much material. That lets bamboo grow very tall without being too heavy. Picking 'catch more sunlight' mixes up the stem's job with the leaf's job.

flow.do: Read the creative ideas and try one of them, or your child's own idea.
flow.say: Can we make the tube even stronger? Try adding rings, like bamboo's nodes.
flow.kid: Try to beat the tube. Add rings like bamboo. Or roll three thin tubes together. Test it!
flow.think: Bicycle frames and the poles that hold up shamianas are tubes too. Why do you think engineers chose the same shape as bamboo?

challenges.context: This is an engineering challenge. You make paper stems in different shapes and test which holds up the most books. It shows why so many plant stems are tubes.

quiz.p: Farhan, a boy in Class 3, cuts all the roots off a small plant and puts the plant back in wet soil. What will most likely happen first?
opts: The plant wilts, because they cannot soak up water
quiz.why: Roots soak up water from the soil. Without roots, the leaves keep losing water but nothing comes in, so the plant goes floppy. Picking 'nothing changes' forgets that the soil water can only get in through roots.

quiz.p: A leaf is covered in thick mud for a week. Which job of the leaf is stopped?
opts: Holding the plant in the soil
Carrying water down to the roots
quiz.why: A leaf catches sunlight to make the plant's food. Mud blocks the light, so the leaf cannot do this. Picking 'holding the plant in the soil' mixes the leaf up with the roots.

quiz.p: Why are roots long, thin and branching?
opts: So they can reach far and touch lots of soil to soak up water
So they can catch light underground
So they are easy for us to eat
quiz.why: Thin roots squeeze between soil grains, and many branches touch far more soil than one fat root could. Picking 'easy to eat' thinks of roots as made for us, not for the plant.

quiz.p: A bean stem is thin and bendy. How does that suit its job?
opts: It can wind round a stick to climb towards the light
It can hold up a heavy crown of branches
It can store lots of food
quiz.why: A thin, bendy stem is perfect for twining round a support. Picking 'hold up a heavy crown' describes a tree trunk, which is thick and woody for that job.

quiz.p: Which clue shows that ginger is a stem, not a root?
quiz.why: Rings are nodes, and buds grow at nodes. Stems have these, and roots usually do not. Picking 'grows underground' is the most common mistake. Roots and stems can both grow underground.

quiz.p: What is an onion's juicy layer?
opts: A swollen leaf that stores food
quiz.why: Each layer is the swollen bottom of a leaf, joined to a tiny flat stem at the base. Picking 'root' decides by where it grows. The real roots are the thin threads underneath.

quiz.p: Why does a carrot plant store food in their root?
opts: To use later to grow a flower stalk and seeds
So that people will eat it
Because the leaves cannot hold any food
To make the root heavy so it does not blow away
quiz.why: A carrot stores food in their root first. Later, after the cold weather, they use that food to grow their flowers and seeds. Picking 'so people will eat it' sees the plant as made for us.

quiz.p: Which of these climbs using tendrils?
quiz.why: Pea plants grab with curly tendrils. A money plant climbs with little roots instead. Picking 'money plant' is close, because they climb, but they use a different tool.

quiz.p: In the Sun Leaf, Shade Leaf test, you counted squares to measure each leaf. Why did we use the middle number of 5 leaves, not just one leaf?
opts: One leaf could be unusual, so the middle of 5 is fairer
Because one leaf would be too small to count
quiz.why: One leaf could be oddly big or small. Testing 5 and taking the middle one gives a fairer answer. Picking 'make the sums harder' misses why scientists repeat tests.
quiz.context: In the Sun Leaf, Shade Leaf experiment, you trace 5 sun leaves and 5 shade leaves from one bush on squared paper and count the squares.

quiz.p: Look at the chart from the Wake the Store test. Which piece grew the tallest shoot?
quiz.why: The onion's bar is the tallest, at 60 mm. Picking the carrot middle means reading the chart upside down. Its bar is at zero, because it grew nothing.
quiz.context: In the Wake the Store experiment, you stand pieces of vegetables in water for 8 days and measure the tallest new shoot on each.

quiz.p: In the Roots Hold the Soil test, what was the one thing we changed?
opts: Whether the tray had grass roots or bare soil
quiz.why: In a fair test you change only one thing. Here, it was the roots. Everything else stayed the same. Picking 'the amount of water' would make the test unfair, because then two things change.
quiz.context: In the Roots Hold the Soil experiment, you pour water over a tilted tray of grass and a tilted tray of bare soil.

quiz.p: Why does a cactus have a fat green stem?
opts: To store water and make food, because their leaves are spines
quiz.why: In the desert, wide leaves would lose too much water. So the cactus's stem stores water and does the leaf's food-making job. Picking 'they have no roots' is wrong: cactuses have roots, often spreading wide to catch rare rain.

quiz.p: Water hyacinth, called jalkumbhi, floats on ponds. Their leaf stalks are swollen and spongy. How does this shape help them?
opts: The spongy stalks are full of air, so the plant floats
The stalks sink the plant to the bottom
quiz.why: The swollen stalks are full of tiny air spaces, like a sponge or a float. So the plant sits on top of the water, where the light is. Picking 'sink the plant' gets it backwards.

quiz.p: Do scientists agree on why leaves are green and not black?
opts: No, it is still an open question
Yes, green catches the most light
quiz.why: It is still argued about. Picking 'green catches the most light' is a common idea. But a leaf lets more green light bounce off than red or blue, and a black leaf would catch more.

quiz.p: What did some of the earliest land plants, about 430 million years ago, look like?
opts: Tiny forked stems with no roots and no leaves
quiz.why: Fossils show the earliest land plants were small stems without roots or leaves. Roots, wide leaves and flowers came much later. Picking 'huge trees' imagines the past like today's forests.

applications: Farmers grow carrot and radish seed by replanting the best roots in winter. This is called the root-to-seed method.
Farmers plant pieces of potato, ginger and sugarcane, each with a bud, to grow new crops without seeds.
Grass and vetiver are planted on slopes and river banks, because their roots hold the soil against rain.
Mangroves are planted along coasts, because their roots break the force of waves and storms.
Khasi and Jaintia people in Meghalaya grow living bridges from the aerial roots of rubber fig trees.
Bamboo stems, strong tubes, are used for scaffolding, ladders, houses and furniture.
Self-cleaning paints and glass copy the bumpy, waxy surface of the lotus leaf.
Gardeners give climbers a support, like a trellis or a string, so they can reach the light.
Sugar is made from sugarcane stems and sugar beet roots, where those plants store their food.
Cooks use turmeric and ginger, two underground stems, in almost every Indian kitchen.
The Crystal Palace, a giant glass building in London in 1851, was designed by a gardener who said the ribs of a giant water lily leaf gave him the idea.

open_questions.q: Why are leaves green and not black?
open_questions.why_open: Black would catch more light. Some scientists think green keeps the energy supply steady. Others think plants simply kept the chlorophyll of their ancestors.

open_questions.q: How does a tendril feel a touch, with no nerves?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists know touch sets off changes inside the tendril's cells within minutes. Exactly how the cells sense it is still being studied.

open_questions.q: Is a gourd's tendril a changed stem or a changed leaf?
open_questions.why_open: Botanists have argued about this for over a hundred years. Recent studies of genes point one way, but not everyone agrees.

open_questions.q: Why do about 9 out of 10 twining plants twist the same way?
open_questions.why_open: It does not depend on which half of the world they grow in. Nobody knows for sure why one direction became so common.

open_questions.q: Why did wide leaves take about 40 million years to become common after plants grew roots?
open_questions.why_open: One idea is that early air had so much carbon dioxide that wide leaves would have overheated. It is still being tested.

open_questions.q: Does light energy travel through a leaf in a strange 'quantum' way?
open_questions.why_open: Some experiments suggested it does, for a very short time. Others say the effect is too short to matter. Scientists still argue.

open_questions.q: How deep can roots really go?
open_questions.why_open: Roots are hidden, so they are hard to measure. The deepest ones are found by chance, in caves, mines and wells.

open_questions.q: What would plants look like on other planets?
open_questions.why_open: We have not found any. Scientists can only make careful guesses from the light of other stars.
