maths.problem: In the Sun Leaf, Shade Leaf test, the middle sun leaf covered 18 squares of 1 cm squared paper. The middle shade leaf covered 27 squares. How many more squares did the shade leaf cover?
maths.explain: Find the difference between the two numbers. 27 take away 18 is 9. You can check by counting on: from 18 to 20 is 2, and from 20 to 27 is 7. 2 + 7 = 9. So the shade leaf covered 9 more squares than the sun leaf.
maths.context: In the Sun Leaf, Shade Leaf experiment, you draw round leaves from the sunny outside and the shady inside of one bush on 1 cm squared paper. Then you count the squares inside each leaf.
maths.why_maths: Counting squares turns 'this leaf looks bigger' into a number. Then we can say exactly how much bigger the shade leaf is.

maths.problem: In the Wake the Store test, the onion's tallest shoot was 12 mm on day 2 and 60 mm on day 8. How much did it grow in those 6 days? About how much is that each day?
maths.answer: It grew 48 mm, which is 8 mm each day.
maths.explain: First find how much it grew. 60 take away 12 is 48 mm. From day 2 to day 8 is 6 days. Share 48 mm equally between 6 days. 48 divided by 6 is 8. So it grew about 8 mm each day. Check: 6 lots of 8 is 48.
maths.context: In the Wake the Store experiment, you stand an onion base in a saucer of water and measure its tallest green shoot every two days.

answer_chart.title: Made-up example: the onion's tallest shoot

maths.why_maths: Taking away tells us how much the shoot grew. Sharing it out by the days tells us how fast it grew, so we can compare it with other plants.

maths.problem: Here are the Wake the Store results after 8 days: onion 60 mm, radish top 55 mm, carrot top 40 mm, potato 15 mm, carrot middle 0 mm. Draw a bar chart. Which piece grew second tallest?
maths.answer: The radish top grew second tallest. Here is the bar chart.
maths.explain: Draw one bar for each piece, as tall as its number. Put the numbers in order from tallest to shortest: 60, 55, 40, 15, 0. The tallest is the onion, at 60 mm. The next is the radish top, at 55 mm. So the radish top is second. The carrot middle gets no bar at all, because it grew 0 mm.
maths.context: In the Wake the Store experiment, you stand pieces of vegetables in water and measure their tallest new shoot after 8 days.

answer_chart.title: Made-up example results: tallest new shoot after 8 days

maths.why_maths: A list of five numbers is hard to compare at a glance. A bar chart shows straight away which store woke up most, and which did not wake at all.

maths.problem: On a pineapple you counted 8 spirals one way and 13 the other. These are in the Fibonacci pattern: 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13. What are the next two numbers?
maths.explain: Each number in the pattern is the two before it added together. 1 + 1 = 2. 1 + 2 = 3. 2 + 3 = 5. 3 + 5 = 8. 5 + 8 = 13. So the next is 8 + 13 = 21. The one after is 13 + 21 = 34. Big sunflower heads often have 34 spirals one way and 55 the other.
maths.context: In the Look Down on a Plant activity, you count the spirals of scales on a pineapple, first going one way and then the other.
maths.why_maths: Spotting the rule in a pattern lets you predict numbers you have not counted yet. Then you can go and check them on a real sunflower or pine cone.

maths.problem: A farmer cuts a seed potato into pieces, so that each piece has one eye. The potato has 6 eyes. Each piece grows into a plant that makes about 5 new potatoes. About how many potatoes will the farmer dig up?
maths.explain: There are 6 pieces, one for each eye. Each piece makes about 5 potatoes. That is 6 groups of 5. 5 + 5 + 5 + 5 + 5 + 5 = 30. Or 6 times 5 is 30. So one potato can become about 30.
maths.context: A potato's eyes are buds. In the Wake the Store experiment, a potato's eyes grow shoots, because they are buds on a stem.
maths.why_maths: Multiplying equal groups shows why farmers count eyes, not potatoes. Every bud on the stem is a whole new plant.

maths.problem: In the Climbing Bean Diary, you and your friends looked down on 10 twining plants. 9 wound anticlockwise and 1 wound clockwise. Make a tally chart. How many more wound anticlockwise than clockwise?
maths.explain: Make a tally mark for each plant. Anticlockwise gets 9 marks: a bundle of five and four more. Clockwise gets 1 mark. 9 take away 1 is 8. So 8 more plants wound anticlockwise. Scientists who counted hundreds of kinds of twining plant found a similar split: about 9 out of every 10 twist the same way.
maths.context: In the Climbing Bean Diary, you look down on a twining bean stem from above, to see whether it winds the same way as a clock's hands or the other way. These numbers are made up.

answer_chart.title: Made-up tally: which way 10 twiners wound, seen from above

maths.why_maths: A tally lets you count as you look, without losing your place. Comparing the totals shows a real pattern that scientists found too.

roots.context: We have been learning how roots, stems and leaves are each shaped for their job. Now we ask what a plant's shape tells us about ourselves and the world.

deep_truth.truth: A potato is a stem and a sweet potato is a root. Yet both are fat, both grow underground, and both are packed with stored food. The same job gave two different parts the same shape. So to tell a stem from a root, look for buds, like the potato's eyes.
deep_truth.habit: We sort things by how they look and where we find them. Fat and underground seems to mean root. But what a part is depends on what it grows from, and its buds show that. Its shape only tells us its job.
deep_truth.evidence: In Vegetable Detectives, the potato has eyes in a spiral and the sweet potato has none. In the Blue-Black Test, both turn blue-black, because both are packed with starch. In Wake the Store, the potato's eyes grow shoots, because they are buds on a stem.

three.who_am_i: Your arm and a bat's wing have the same bones inside, shaped for different jobs. So the same kind of part can take very different shapes.
three.what_is_life: A plant grows each part to suit its job and its place. A shade leaf grows bigger than a sun leaf on the same plant.
three.what_is_this_world: In the world, things that do the same job often end up looking alike, even when they started out different.

roots.thread: Every plant begins as one single cell. That cell divides again and again, first into the tiny plant inside a seed, then into the whole plant. Their cells become roots, stems, leaves, tendrils, spines and petals, each shaped for its job. One life takes many forms, and a single plant shows this inside one body. You also grew from one cell, into hands, eyes and ears.

teachings.teaching: Uddalaka asks his son to split a banyan seed. 'What do you see?' 'Nothing.' From that unseen nothing, a great banyan tree grows.
teachings.link: Inside a seed you cannot see a root, a stem or a leaf. Yet all of them grow from the seed, each with its own shape.

teachings.source: Udana 6.4, a Buddhist text. Jain teachers tell the same story to explain anekantavada, many-sidedness
teachings.teaching: Blind men each touch one part of an elephant. One feels an ear and says an elephant is like a winnowing basket, a soop. Another feels a leg and says an elephant is like a pillar. Each is partly right, and each is wrong about the whole.
teachings.link: One clue can fool us. Underground and fat makes a potato seem like a root. Botanists look at many clues together, like buds, rings and what the part grows from.

teachings.source: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe, The Metamorphosis of Plants (1790)
teachings.teaching: Goethe, a German poet, believed every part of a flower is a changed leaf. One basic form takes many shapes.
teachings.link: Petals and pea tendrils really are changed leaves. Here very different shapes turn out to be the same kind of part.

science.text: Cactuses in America and spiny euphorbias in Africa are not related, but both grew fat, green, spiny stems in dry places. Biologists call this convergent evolution: unrelated living things grow alike because they live in a similar way.
A few genes decide whether a part grows as a leaf, a petal or a stamen. Switch them off, and a flower grows only leaf-like parts (Coen and Meyerowitz, 1991).

other_view.who: Rolf Sattler, a Canadian botanist, and others who study plant shape
other_view.view: They say root, stem and leaf are boxes people made. Many real plant parts sit between the boxes, partly stem and partly leaf. So asking 'is it really a stem?' may not always have one answer.

how_we_found_out.context: Are a flower's petals a new kind of part, or leaves in another shape? This card tells the true story of how scientists found out.
how_we_found_out.story: In 1790 the German poet and thinker Johann Wolfgang von Goethe wrote a short book about plants. He had noticed parts that were halfway between a leaf and a petal. He guessed that every part of a flower is a leaf that has changed shape. Many botanists treated petals, stamens and leaves as completely different kinds of part. For about 200 years nobody could test Goethe's guess properly. Then, in the 1980s, scientists studied flowers that had grown wrongly. Enrico Coen and Rosemary Carpenter in England worked on snapdragons. Elliot Meyerowitz and his team in America worked on a small weed called thale cress. In some odd flowers, petals grew where the stamens should be. In 1991, Coen and Meyerowitz explained it. A few genes, working together, decide what each part of a flower becomes. When scientists switched off three of these genes, the flower grew only green, leaf-like parts. In 2001, Takashi Honma and Koji Goto in Japan did the reverse. They switched these genes on in ordinary leaves, and the leaves grew like petals.
how_we_found_out.who: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe (1790); Enrico Coen and Rosemary Carpenter in England, and Elliot Meyerowitz and his team in America (1980s to 1991); Takashi Honma and Koji Goto in Japan (2001)
how_we_found_out.when: Goethe's idea in 1790; the flower genes explained in 1991; leaves turned into petals in 2001
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: That petals, stamens and leaves are completely different kinds of part. Flowers with changed genes showed that they are all built on the plan of a leaf, and a few genes decide which shape each one takes. Goethe also went too far: some sharp points, like bougainvillea thorns, are changed branches, not leaves.
how_we_found_out.art: A row of flowers: an ordinary snapdragon, an odd one with extra petals where the stamens should be, and one made only of small green leaf-like parts, with a leaf turned petal-coloured at the end.
